title: Low-Overhead Quantum Error Correction with Boundary-Connected Planar Modules
abstract: Realizing practical quantum computers requires quantum error correction, but the most widely implemented approach, the planar surface code, demands a substantial physical qubit overhead. Here, we demonstrate that partitioning quantum processors into manageable, flat modules with non-local inter-module connections provides a natural solution. By wiring sparse, static boundary connections between Euclidean planar modules, we construct modular hyperbolic surface and color codes, based on new families of semi-hyperbolic codes. Using modular syndrome extraction circuits and efficient neural network and matching decoders, our circuit-level simulations show that this modular memory design can reduce the physical qubit overhead by tenfold or more compared to the surface code, even under elevated inter-module seam error rates. Projecting to larger system sizes, we find modular codes with encoding rate $k/n=1/16$ and distance $d\geq 22$, exceeding both the rate and distance of the $[[288,12,18]]$ two-gross bivariate bicycle code while using mostly nearest-neighbor gates within planar modules, and implying an over $30\times$ overhead reduction relative to surface codes. We develop fault-tolerant walking circuits for implementing logic via code automorphisms, which we co-design with low-weight, highly symmetrical logical bases and a modular extractor system that is $\approx 4.5\times$ smaller than the code itself. Combining these methods, our modular memory can be used as dense storage in a universal fault-tolerant architecture, unlocking the efficiency of high-rate codes without sacrificing the fabrication advantages of planar modules.
summary:
**TL;DR** The authors build hyperbolic surface and color codes out of flat, surface-code-like planar modules (~70–120 qubits each) joined only by sparse, static long-range couplers at module boundaries, so that all negative curvature lives in the inter-module "seams." Circuit-level simulations with SI1000 noise at p=0.1% and 10× noisier seam gates (p_seam=1%) show ~10× fewer physical qubits per logical qubit than the surface code at a 1e-10 logical error rate, extrapolating to >30× (36 physical qubits per logical at distance 20–24), together with a logical-control scheme combining code automorphisms and a modular "ribbon extractor."

**The big picture** High-rate quantum error-correcting codes promise far cheaper fault tolerance than the surface code, but they typically demand dense, long, crossing wiring that is hard to fabricate on a chip. Meanwhile, chips must be split into modules anyway because of yield and size limits. This work shows that the module boundaries are exactly where the small number of exotic connections should go: each chip stays a flat, locally standard patch, and the handful of cables between chips supplies the curved geometry that gives the high encoding rate. The result is close to an order of magnitude or more saving in qubits, using hardware ingredients superconducting labs have already demonstrated separately.

**Key contributions**
- New families of semi-hyperbolic surface codes (qubits on dual-lattice vertices, rotated-surface-code style, balancing X/Z distance and allowing uniform module partitions) and, for the first time, semi-hyperbolic *color* codes via fine-graining triangular hyperbolic tilings with Euclidean hexagonal patches.
- Module partitions derived from the base tiling (quadrilateral/octagon for color codes), making each module a flat Euclidean tile with purely nearest-neighbor internal gates.
- Modular syndrome extraction: Bell-pair + flag measurement in the bulk, GHZ/cat states across seams, and multi-rate schedules measuring seam stabilizers once per three rounds — tolerant of slow, 10× noisier inter-module gates.
- Decoding with a retrained AlphaQubit variant (color codes) and correlated MWPM (surface codes).
- Logical control: symmetric canonical homology bases whose cycles lie in a single automorphism orbit (100 of 104 logicals for [[6400,104,30]]), O(L)-depth SWAP "walking" circuits implementing tiling rotations with one extra coupler seam per module side, and a distance-preserving modular ribbon extractor (~4.5× smaller than the memory, +22% qubits) measuring all 15 nontrivial products of four logicals on a cycle.
- A compiled 50-bit ripple-carry adder benchmark: 21,402 / 28,930 QEC cycles on the [[3600,104,22]] / [[6400,104,30]] memories.

**How it works** A closed hyperbolic surface from a triangle or quadrilateral Coxeter group is tiled, each face replaced by an L×L Euclidean patch; k is unchanged, d grows ~L, n grows ~L², preserving kd²/n while flattening locality. Automorphisms are rotations of the tiling that permute modules, letting one extractor reach hundreds of logical Paulis by teleporting operators under it in ≤6 moves (mean 4.4).

**Why it matters** It reframes modularity from a liability into the enabling resource for high-rate QLDPC codes, and claims better rate *and* distance than the two-gross bivariate bicycle code with mostly 2D-local connectivity — directly relevant to superconducting roadmaps.

**Caveats** The headline >30× figure comes from extrapolation to larger system sizes, not direct simulation. Walking-circuit cost is assessed only through a simplified stabilizer-dislocation model. Ribbon extractors are demonstrated only for quadrilateral-partition color codes. Real-time, sub-distance-parallel decoding remains unsolved, defect tolerance is assumed adaptable rather than shown, and no end-to-end algorithm resource estimate is given.

title: Scalable Passive QRAM

\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
    We present a blueprint for implementing the physical QRAM operation in a scalable, passive manner, proving its feasibility in principle. Our construction is passive because for an $n$-qubit address over $N = 2^n$ memory bits the energy cost per QRAM query is $O(\log N)$, and to our knowledge it is the first construction to use $\polylog N$ energy. The runtime for each query is $O(\log^2 N)$. It is achieved by evolving a pre-manufactured time-independent 4-local Hamiltonian with $O(N)$ terms where every qubit participates in at most 4 terms.
\end{abstract}
\section{Introduction}
 
The three decades of quantum algorithms research since Shor's factoring algorithm~\cite{Shor97} have coincided with the ascendancy of big data and machine learning. Yet the most promising candidates for practical quantum advantage lie firmly in the \textit{small}-data regime. For example, the input to a 2048-bit RSA factoring instance fits on a single sheet of paper. Mapping the phase diagram of the Fermi--Hubbard model 
\cite{qin2022hubbard} requires only a handful of inputs, such as the interaction strength $U/t$, filling, temperature, and lattice geometry. And computing the ground-state energy of FeMoco, a standard benchmark, involves a Hamiltonian with only about 180,000 unique coefficients (after truncating near-zero terms)~\cite{Berry2019qubitizationof}; tellingly, later improvements in gate count \cite{vonBurg2021computationalCatalysis,lee2021THC,caesura2025fasterQuantumChemistry,low2025fastQuantumSimulation} came precisely from precomputing factorizations that compress and reshape this input.

The cost of quantum data loading constitutes a fundamental headwind relative to classical methods, which access these small inputs with ease. Is quantum computing destined to remain confined to a niche of ``small-data, big-compute'' problems? A key part of the answer, we believe, lies in an asymmetry between classical and quantum random access memory (RAM and QRAM). Classical algorithms can access massive datasets cheaply because memory access is \textit{passive}. Conventional quantum data access, by contrast, is inherently active and incurs a gate cost that grows linearly with input size~\cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}. This disparity in data loading makes big-data applications essentially dead on arrival as candidates for practical quantum advantage.

\paragraph{This work.} Our main contribution is to provide a blueprint for implementing QRAM passively at the physical level. The blueprint departs from the conventional gate-based paradigm of quantum computing and supports an alternative vision for how quantum computers may one day tackle data-intensive computational problems. The construction is hardware agnostic and abstract, but possesses several features such as robustness to noise which suggest that a scalable, passive QRAM is possible at least in principle. 

\input{figs/ram_chip_sram}

\paragraph{Passive RAM.}
It is instructive to recall an abstract picture of how classical RAM works. For a dataset of size $N$, a circuit with $O(N)$ elements is physically printed on the chip at fabrication time. As depicted in \cref{fig:ram-chip}, a query is initiated by setting voltages on $O(\log N)$ address pins, after which only a small fraction of the $O(N)$ elements \emph{switch} in response, autonomously routing the requested data to the output pins through a circuit of only $O(\log N)$ logical depth. In asynchronous memories, the requested data simply appears at the output a fixed propagation time after the address is set---in practice just a handful of nanoseconds. No element requires individual external control, and elements that do not switch dissipate no dynamic energy, so the energy expended by a query scales sublinearly with $N$. In an idealized circuit model, total energy dissipated can be as little as $\polylog N$, though practical memories laid out as two-dimensional arrays switch an entire row of cells on each access.  These two properties---no individual control and negligible energy for idle elements---make it possible to shrink the elements and pack them at enormous density, so memory capacity has grown by many orders of magnitude while the cost of each query has grown only weakly with the size of the data. Accordingly, the standard cost model for classical algorithms treats each memory query as a unit-cost operation, regardless of how much data is stored.

\paragraph{QRAM and its challenges.} QRAM is a theoretical primitive that generalizes the task performed by RAM: it allows rapid access to an arbitrary location in a massive memory, and is augmented with the ability to query this memory in \emph{superposition}. Inspired by RAM, quantum algorithms designers commonly model QRAM as a unit-cost operation. In fact, this ``cheap QRAM'' assumption is required to realize quantum advantage with superposition queries to an arbitrary oracle without a succint implementation~\cite{Grover96,BernsteinVazirani,Kuperberg13,AAForrelation}. 

But it remains contentious to make this assumption,
because we do not have a compelling plan for how to implement this superposition access to classical memory in a scalable fashion on quantum computers.
Toward this end, the famous bucket-brigade circuit~\cite{GLL08} makes some progress. It implements QRAM access to memories of size $N$ in depth $\polylog N$ while ``switching'' only $\polylog N$ components, resembling how a RAM query switches only a small fraction of its circuit elements. However, the configuration of switched components  is a superposition spanning the whole device, entangled with the address. Thus, to operate the circuit one still has to apply a quantum gate to actively \emph{check} (via application of a quantum gate) whether each component should be switched, which needs $\Omega(N)$ interventions from classical control and expends $\Omega(N)$ energy. This conclusion is difficult to avoid since any circuit for QRAM requires $\Omega(N)$ gates, and in the dominant paradigm for quantum computing, information processing is done actively by applying pulses or other interventions. 
Assuming cheap access to QRAM was one of the main concerns raised in an essay by Aaronson~\cite{Aaronson2015ReadTF} which asked readers to be careful about claimed quantum speedups for machine learning applications~\cite{HHL09,Childs2009-mk,wiebe2015quantumdeeplearning,LloydMohseniRebentrost2013,RebentrostMohseniLloyd2014,WiebeBraunLloyd2012,GarneroneZanardiLidar2012}. Outside of quantum machine learning, availability of QRAM would also lead to better algorithms for dihedral HSP~\cite{Kuperberg13}.
More generally, it would address the main challenge
in quantum applications~\cite{babbush2025grandchallengequantumapplications}, by enabling us to take algorithms from abstract advantages in oracle-models to ensembles of inputs where we can demonstrate quantum advantage.
In particular, with QRAM we would not require a streaming model to achieve quantum advantage for big-data problems~\cite{zhao2026exponentialquantumadvantageprocessing}.
The challenge of implementing QRAM is well-documented~\cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}, wherein the passive approach to QRAM was defined but considered challenging, presented along with partial impossibility results.
We thus solve the main open question from this survey in \cref{thm:main}, circumventing their impossibility results.

\paragraph{What we mean by passive.} We say that a proposal for QRAM is \emph{passive} if it uses $\polylog N$ energy per query to a memory of size $N$, as opposed to the $\Omega(N)$ energy it would naively take to implement the full circuit, following \cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}.
We take the perspective that achieving a passive QRAM requires designing a time-independent Hamiltonian which implements the QRAM query autonomously, as posed in \cite[Section 6.3]{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}. Since this Hamiltonian ``naturally'' implements the routing and read operations, this process consumes no energy. 
The energy consumption thus comes only from initializing and resetting the qubits the Hamiltonian acts on.  Another benefit of this approach is that, since gates are performed autonomously, in principle it removes the need to allocate individual control lines for each component of the device, an important bottleneck in scaling up quantum hardware~\cite{franke2019rent,kennedy2026designoperationwaferscalepackages}.

It's not obvious this circumvents the energy bottleneck because the Hamiltonian must necessarily have a $\Omega(N)$ size workspace, and all those qubits may need to be reset after every query. This also means that the number of \emph{terms} in the Hamiltonian must be $\Omega(N)$. 
Although this means a linear cost at the time of manufacturing, this is an unavoidable one-time cost, and also true of classical RAM. Thus, we only care about the cost per query. We show that our construction only needs $O(\log N)$ qubits to be reset on every query, giving us a passive QRAM. This circumvents the barrier shown by~\cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}, which shows that a Hamiltonian that implements QRAM must have spectral norm $\Omega(N)$. Our construction does indeed have large spectral norm, but it is a quantum many-body system with $\Omega(N)$ modes and only $\polylog N$ excitations which hop around in those modes, which still results in $\polylog N$ energy consumption.

\paragraph{What we mean by scalable.} For the QRAM Hamiltonian to be manufactured at scale, the construction should break down into a finite number of hardware \emph{primitives} that repeat many times to build the Hamiltonian. Further, the complexity of the primitive should scale mildly with $N$, which we model as $\polylog N$. For example, this means that as $N$ grows, we should only need to implement the primitives with imprecision $1/\polylog N$ as opposed to $1/N$. Our Hamiltonian construction is given in terms of these primitives, and our noise resilience results confirm that these primitives only need to be manufactured with mildly small imprecision. At a high level, our Hamiltonian is noise resilient because the primitives are arranged as a binary tree  as in the bucket-brigade protocol~\cite{Giovannetti2008Architectures, HannNoise21}. Thus, any errors in one branch of the tree do not affect the other branches in a meaningful way.

We are thus ready to state our main result. We state an informal result which is a consequence of our construction in \cref{thm:exact qram} and the statement of \cref{thm:intro-noise}.

\begin{mainresult}(Informal)
\label{thm:main}
    An asymptotically scalable passive QRAM which evolves a time-independent Hamiltonian is feasible in principle. For $n$-qubit queries over $N = 2^n$ bits, the energy cost per query is $O(\log N)$ and the runtime is $O(\log^2 N)$. Moreover, queries can be executed with constant error even if there is $1/\polylog N$ imprecision in each component.
\end{mainresult}

\input{figs/qram_chip}

Our construction is visualized in \cref{fig:qram-chip}. The address and bus qubits are encoded in unary (dual-rail), and can be initialized into an arbitrary superposition. The query is initiated by exciting the auxiliary qubit labeled ``start.'' At exactly a specific $\Theta(\log^2 N)$ amount of time later, the query completes: the address and bus register are returned having picked up the corresponding data bit in the bus, and the excitation that began in the start register is now in the register labeled ``end.'' Active control only acts on the $O(\log N)$ qubits depicted as circles in the figure: at the beginning to initialize and set off the evolution, and at the end to retrieve the answer and halt the evolution.

\paragraph{Locality and degree.}
When designing a Hamiltonian, we need to assign constraints to make it feasible to physically manufacture it. We optimize for two fundamental parameters of the Hamiltonian: its locality (how many qubits participate in each term), and the degree of its interaction hypergraph induced by the terms (how many terms a qubit participates in).

We are able to achieve very simple 4-local interactions. While our construction is agnostic to any specific platform, this is particularly compelling in the context of superconducting qubits because the famous Josephson junction~\cite{Josephson1962,MDCa,MDCb,MDCc} can create fairly general 4-body interactions with standard components.
Having numerous Hamiltonian terms which are 5-local or worse would introduce significant engineering complexity.
Along with the few-body interactions, we also have maximum qubit degree 4. This is useful because platforms like superconducting circuits have practical limits on how many neighbors a given qubit can interact with, for example because each additional coupling adds capacitance and occupies space around the qubit, and increases frequency crowding and crosstalk.

\paragraph{Integration into a fault-tolerant quantum algorithm.} 

Furthermore, a noisy physical QRAM operation implemented by this blueprint can be useful within a fault-tolerant quantum computation using the distillation--teleportation protocol of~\cite{Dalzell2025DistillationTeleportationFTQRAM}.
The logical QRAM operation on a memory of size $N$ can be accomplished up to arbitrary $1/\polylog N$ error with $\polylog N$ queries to our blueprint passive QRAM device and $\polylog N$ other fault-tolerant gates. Thus, our work and \cite{Dalzell2025DistillationTeleportationFTQRAM} together show that logical QRAM can incur only $\polylog N$ total quantum cost (in terms of energy). However, achieving fault tolerance with the distillation--teleportation approach of \cite{Dalzell2025DistillationTeleportationFTQRAM} still incurs at least $\Omega(N)$ purely classical cost for adaptive memory updates.  Thus, we do not achieve ``strongly passive'' QRAM,  as defined in \cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique, zhang2026bitsqubitstheorypractice}, which requires $o(N)$ complexity across the whole stack, including classical computation. We have also therefore \textit{not} yet fully justified the cheap QRAM assumption used in the analysis of quantum algorithms. Nevertheless, our construction supports the conclusion that physical QRAM need not be a barrier in this research program. 

\paragraph{Outline and Outlook.} We believe this is a reasonable proposal for passive physical QRAM. It formally avoids the linear energy cost of any active approach, and it mirrors the operation of passive classical RAM as in \cref{fig:ram-chip}. With low enough imprecision in fabrication, and a suitable layout of the qubits and interaction terms, this blueprint could be realized on any platform that would support such a passive Hamiltonian evolution. Candidates include superconducting and silicon photonic architectures.  In contrast,  neutral atom and trapped ion architectures appear less compatible since active energy input is required for trapping in proportion to the number of atoms/ions. 

Our approach differs from previous experimental proposals or implementations~\cite{GLL08,Jaques2025qramsurveycritique,miaoetalqrouter,Shen2026BucketBrigade} in the crucial aspect that we first construct an abstract Hamiltonian encoding the circuit which is reminiscent of the Feynman-Kitaev clock constructions to synchronize the time evolution of different gates.
Previous QRAM proposals did not perform routing passively, and hence consumed energy linear in memory size.
The technical novelty in our construction is to specialize the clock construction to QRAM which allows us to optimize many parameters.
We state our results in \cref{sec:our_results} below. In \cref{sec:hamiltonian} we focus on defining a time-independent Hamiltonian satisfying the conditions of \cref{thm:exact qram}. 
\Cref{sec:experiment} discusses a proposal of how one would manufacture this Hamiltonian with our current knowledge of hardware, although our construction is agnostic to any platform or hardware type. In \cref{sec:noise} we focus on how to avoid resetting an exponential number of qubits on every query, and how to deal with imprecision during manufacturing and runtime. 
Combining these results, we have a proposal for passive QRAM. There is work to be done to figure out the best platform, the best embedding of the Hamiltonian into 2D or 3D space, to figure out how to engineer the 4-body couplings needed for this Hamiltonian at scale, and to deal with the long range 2-body interactions as explained in \cref{sec:experiment}. Note that via lightcone arguments \cite{wang2024fundamental} the long-range interactions are unavoidable, indeed this is the case even in classical RAM. But we remain hopeful because in practice the speed of light is not a bottleneck.

For silicon-based platforms, there is also the bottleneck of the largest wafer that could be manufactured with existing technology.  There is a practical limit of how close we could put two Hamiltonian terms but superconducting architectures have demonstrated sites less than 1 micron apart~\cite{Macha2014QuantumMetamaterial}, and recent works on spin qubits have demonstrated less than 100 nanometers~\cite{Philips2022SixQubitSilicon,HRL2026SiliconQPU}.
The largest wafers manufactured with an industrial process is about 300mm in diameter~\cite{Van_Damme2024-eq}. This lets us get up to $n = 32$ conservatively, corresponding to 500 MiB of QRAM. In classical hardware, memory sizes have grown because components have miniaturized and become extremely dense, and we may hope this will be repeated for quantum hardware as well. 
For $N=2^{32}$ and assuming operating frequencies typical for superconducting qubits (around 5 GHz), a back of the envelope calculation suggests that a temperature of 14mK is sufficient to keep enough of system in their ground state at initialization for the overall query error to be less than 10\%. 
This is around the temperature at which dilution refrigerators are operated for superconducting hardware.
This makes QRAM with memory $\approx 500$MB conceivable, acknowledging several theoretical (such as exact qubit layout) and experimental (such as long-range Hamiltonian terms) ingredients still remain to be specified.
We leave the details of choosing the best platform and fabricating the passive Hamiltonian for future work and 
hope that this encourages interest in the realization of scalable passive QRAM.

\subsection{Related work}
Prior work deals with three questions that are easy to blur together: (i) how to route a
coherent address on hardware, (ii) how to make the query autonomous, and (iii) how errors scale with the
memory size.

\paragraph{Routing and hardware.}
Giovannetti, Lloyd, and Maccone introduced the fanout and bucket-brigade
architectures~\cite{GLL08,Giovannetti2008Architectures}. A bucket-brigade
device contains $\Theta(N)$ routers arranged in a depth-$n$ binary tree, but only the $n$ routers corresponding to a path from root to leaf store
the address in each computational-basis branch. Their concrete cavity scheme
still loads the address, routes the bus, and erases the path with a timed
sequence of pulses. This is inherently an active implementation of QRAM and requires $\Omega(N)$ energy to implement.
More recent superconducting experiments have implemented an addressable router~\cite{miaoetalqrouter} and circuit-based bucket-brigade
memories with four and eight data bits~\cite{Shen2026BucketBrigade}. These
works test active routing primitives. They do not implement a query by free
evolution under one fixed Hamiltonian. Our construction is also \emph{passive} in this sense: after the inputs are prepared and the query begins, the
couplings stay fixed until readout.

\paragraph{Hamiltonian formulation.}
Jaques and Rattew sharpen the distinction between active and passive
QRAM~\cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}. An external controller cannot learn
which branches support a coherent address, so an active protocol must be
ready to control all $\Theta(N)$ routers.
This motivates a time-independent Hamiltonian construction which implements QRAM queries
(or at least one with few active interventions).
But so far, there has been no satisying solution which builds a device whose couplers are built
once and whose idle state is perturbed to begin a query. A time-independent Hamiltonian approach was considered in Asaka, Sakai, and Yahagi~\cite{quantumwalkers1,quantumwalkers2}. But their proposal is not known to be scalable or passive. We do not know how to prove noise resilience gaurantees for their proposal.
Bohac gives another time-independent QRAM
Hamiltonian but it has interaction degree $\Theta(N)$~\cite{Bohac2025UniversalQRAM}.

Feynman, Kitaev, and later works give circuit-to-Hamiltonian constructions~\cite{feynman1986quantum,
kitaev1997quantum,Nagaj2010}. The space-time construction of Breuckmann and
Terhal also encodes the parallelism of the circuit in a local
Hamiltonian~\cite{BB14}. Applied directly to QRAM, a sequential clock follows
the $\Theta(N)$ gates of the routing circuit, while the space-time
construction targets a history state rather than exact transfer to the
output at a prescribed time. Our construction instead uses the tree
structure of bucket brigade. Each basis query sees one path, and perfect
state transfer along that path~\cite{Christandl2004} produces the output
exactly after $O(n^2)$ time.

Our Hamiltonian
may couple distant qubits, so it does not evade the causal bounds for
finite-range interactions proved by Wang et al.~\cite{Wang2024CausalQRAM}.

\paragraph{Noise.}
Hann et al.\ proved local-noise resilience for the bucket-brigade circuit~\cite{HannNoise21}. Their key observation is branch isolation, that is, an error at one router affects only address branches that visit it. They consider a qutrit implementation such that the infidelity of the output of their circuit is
$O(\epsilon\log^2 N)$ with the ideal query state, under their local-channel error model where every router suffers an error with probability $\epsilon$. They also give a
two-query protocol that tolerates arbitrary initialization. We prove a
continuous-time version of branch isolation and bound the channel induced by tracing out the qubits beside the address and the bus
in diamond norm. Since the models are different, neither result subsumes the other.

\subsection{Our results}

\label{sec:our_results}
Let $N=2^n$. We have $N$ classical bits of data encoded by $D=(D_x)_{x\in\bits^n}$, stored in memory qubits $M_x$ as $\ket{D_x}$.  The address register is $A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n)$ and the bus is one qubit $B$.  The target QRAM unitary $U$ does not modify the classical data $D$ and can be written as 
\begin{align}
    U = \sum_D U_D \otimes \ket{D}\bra{D}_M\,,\label{eq:qram_U}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}
    U_D \ket a_A\ket b_B
    =\ket a_A\ket{b\xor D_a}_B,
    \qquad a\in\bits^n,\; b\in\bits .
    \label{eq:xor-qram}
\end{equation}
We construct a Hamiltonian where each term involves at most 4 qubits and each qubit participates in at most 4 terms, which implements this unitary. The Hamiltonian acts on $O(N)$ auxiliary qubits in addition to the registers specified in \cref{eq:xor-qram}. This Hamiltonian is independent of $D$ and only requires the memory register as an initial state. To initiate a query, we set the auxiliary register to $\ket{\blacktriangleright}_{\textrm{aux}}$ which has a special `begin' qubit in $\ket{1}$ and all other qubits in $\ket{0}$. Then it evolves for a fixed $\poly(n)$ time. 

\begin{theorem}[Passive Hamiltonian QRAM]
\label{thm:exact qram}
For every $n\ge 1$ there is a time-independent, data-independent Hamiltonian $H_n$ acting on $O(N)$ physical qubits such that,
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.15em]
    \item $H_n$ is $4$-local,
    \item its interaction hypergraph has degree 4,
    \item $e^{-iH_n\tau} \ket{a}_A \ket{b}_B \ket{D}_M \ket{\blacktriangleright}_{\textrm{aux}}$ at $\tau=O(n^2) = O(\log^2 N)$ implements $U$ from~\eqref{eq:qram_U} up to a global phase independent of $a,b,D$ after tracing out the auxiliary qubits.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Note that by a lightcone argument, this Hamiltonian cannot be geometrically local in 2D or 3D while having a $\poly(n)$ runtime \cite{wang2024fundamental}. But we will show how to realize all the geometrically nonlocal terms as simple 2-body interactions, which we expect will be scalable. We now make three claims about the resilience of $H_n$ to noise. We assume that the $M$ register storing the classical data $\ket{D}$ does not experience any noise and does not support superpositions. The ideal QRAM channel $\mathcal{U}$ acts on such states as 
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{U}[\rho_{AB} \otimes \ket{D}\bra{D}] = \mathcal{U}_D[\rho_{AB}] \otimes \ket{D}\bra{D}\,,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{U}_D[\cdot] = U_D[\cdot]U_D^\dagger$. The channel $\mathcal{E}$ realized when noise is included is defined similarly. 
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{E}[\rho_{AB} \otimes \ket{D}\bra{D}_M] = \mathcal{E}_D[\rho_{AB}] \otimes \ket{D}\bra{D}\,,
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{E}_D$ is the noisy channel conditional on $D$.

\begin{theorem}[Noise resilience guarantee]
\label{thm:intro-noise}

For the Hamiltonian $H_n$ in \cref{thm:exact qram} augmented with a 1-local pinning Hamiltonain $P_n$. Then for one query ($m=1$),
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.15em]
\item {\bf Thermal initialization.}
Prepare the $O(\log N)$ address qubits and the bus cleanly, and initialize the remaining qubits thermally from $K_n = H_n + P_n$. Then $\|\mathcal E_{D}-\mathcal U_D\|_\diamond\le \varepsilon$ once $\beta\ge \Omega(\log \log N + \log (1/\varepsilon))$.

Here $\beta$ is the inverse temperature and $g$ is the effective energy gap of a single qubit. At fixed gap $g$ and $\varepsilon = 1/\polylog N$ this is a temperature $T=O(1/\log\log N)$.

\item {\bf Sensitivity to Hamiltonian terms.} Suppose the realized Hamiltonian is
$\widetilde{K}_n=K_n+\sum_\alpha E_\alpha$. Let $\lambda_{\rm err}$ be the maximum sum of spectral norms of the erroneous terms acting on a single qubit. Then $\|\mathcal E_{D}-\mathcal U_D\|_\diamond\le \varepsilon$ if $\lambda_{\rm err} = O(\varepsilon/\log^4 N)$.
\end{enumerate}

These results extend to arbitrary $m$ for $\beta\ge \Omega(\log \log N + \log (m/\varepsilon))$ and $\lambda_{\rm err}  = O(\varepsilon/m^2 \log^4 N)$.
\end{theorem}

We prove (i) in \cref{sec:thermal} and (ii) in \cref{sec:imperfect}. Note that (i) is important for passive QRAM, and (ii) is important for scalable QRAM. We also extend the proof of (ii) to show resilience against continuous Markovian noise, formalized as a Lindbladian~\cite{GKS1976,Lindblad1976}, in \cref{sec:dynamical}.

\subsection{Open questions}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Can we achieve passive QRAM with better tradeoff for parameters? The relevant axes are the runtime, the energy consumption, the sensitivity to Hamiltonian terms, and the resilience to continuous noise. While we achieve $\polylog N$ scaling on all axes, we note that we have not optimized the scaling in favor of more general results. It is possible there is a better combination of tradeoffs, and we expect that for most platforms the noise resilience will be the bottleneck.
    \item Our construction could conceivably be implemented on multiple physical platforms. What are the tradeoffs between different platforms and which ones are the most promising?
    \item Our proposal can be integrated into a fault-tolerant algorithm using the distillation-teleportation protocol of \cite{Dalzell2025DistillationTeleportationFTQRAM}. While this protocol has $\polylog N$ quantum overhead, it has $\Omega(N)$ overhead from classical control. Is there a different protocol which can get $\polylog N$ overhead for both?
\end{itemize}

\section{Technical overview}
We first discuss the construction of the time-independent Hamiltonian whose evolution implements \cref{eq:qram_U}. Our goals will be to optimize the locality of the Hamiltonian (how many qubits participate in each term), the degree of the interaction hypergraph induced by the terms (how many terms a qubit participates in), and the evolution time for getting good overlap with the QRAM state, which we want to be $\poly(n)$.

Later, we discuss how we can avoid a reset of exponentially many qubits on every query and active error correction to make the proposal truly passive. Put together, our results resolve the question of how to build passive QRAM (in principle) despite the no-go results proved in a recent survey on QRAM~\cite{Jaques2025qramsurveycritique}. In their survey, they showed that any Hamiltonian implementation of QRAM must have spectral norm which scales as $\Omega(N)$, which they posed as a barrier to implementing passive QRAM. Our Hamiltonian construction indeed has this property, but it only consumes $O(\log N)$ energy. One explanation of this is that during evolution it stays in a low-energy subspace of the entire Hilbert space. 

\subsection{Hamiltonian construction}
Our starting point for this construction is the original bucket-brigade protocol~\cite{GLL08}. The address bits descend through a branching tree one by one and set a path to the chosen memory cell.
The bus follows that path, reads the stored value, returns. Then the path resets or uncomputes. This is visualized in \cref{fig:bucket-brigade}.
Our aim is to encode this computation in a $O(1)$-local, $O(1)$-degree time-independent Hamiltonian where a $\poly(n)$ time evolution gives us a good overlap with the query output state. We can always use the Feynman-Kitaev (FK) circuit-to-Hamiltonian construction~\cite{feynman1986quantum,kitaev1997quantum}, which gives us a 5-local Hamiltonian, but this has two problems for us. First, the QRAM circuit has \(2^n\poly(n)\) gates, so a sequential clock follows an exponentially large circuit and can have large degree. Second, the usual history-state constructions do not put the final state at a known time with unit fidelity. Our construction uses the tree structure to solve both problems.

Note that there are few circuit-to-Hamiltonian constructions in literature which try to incorporate the parallelization in a circuit into the Hamiltonian construction, most notably the Space-time circuit-to-Hamiltonian
construction~\cite{BB14}. Another example, which deviates strongly from the FK framework, is the tensor network approach of Anshu, Breuckmann, and Nguyen \cite{anshu2024circuitToHamiltonian}. But to the best of our knowledge, none of them give Hamiltonian which outputs a state with good overlap with the QRAM state with $\poly(n)$ evolution time and constant degree.

\paragraph{Evolution time \& fidelity.}
Most constructions of circuit-to-Hamiltonian maps are designed so that the history state is the \emph{ground state} of the Hamiltonian, which is not efficient to passively recover from the Hamiltonian evolution in general. This is not an issue in the setting of proving \QMA-completeness of local Hamiltonian problem, since we just need to run verification given a quantum state which is claimed to be the ground state. But for our purposes we want small evolution time (efficient in the sense of \BQP) and high fidelity with the output state of the circuit. If one were to try and recover the ground state of the FK Hamiltonian,
the evolution time needed to get good overlap with the history state can be exponential in the input size even for Hamiltonians corresponding to polynomial size circuits.
While the QRAM circuit has depth $\poly(n)$ it has size $2^n \cdot \poly(n)$.

\paragraph{Perfect state transfer.} We achieve both of our goals of $\poly(n)$ time evolution and $O(1)$-degree by using the \emph{tree} structure of the QRAM circuit. We construct a Hamiltonian based on perfect state transfer~\cite{Christandl2004}, which corresponds to a 1D nearest-neighbor Hamiltonian of length $L+1$. Let $\sigma^+_j = \ket{1}\!\bra{0}_j$ and $\sigma^-_j = \ket{0}\!\bra{1}_j$ denote raising and lowering operators on site $j$ (which act trivially on the other $L$ sites). Then the perfect state transfer Hamiltonian can be written as
\begin{align}
H_{\rm PST} &= \sum_{j=1}^{L} J_j (\sigma^+_j \sigma^-_{j+1} + \sigma^+_{j+1} \sigma^-_{j})\label{eq:PST}\\
    J_j&=\frac{\Omega}{2}\sqrt{j(L-j+1)},
    \qquad
    \Omega=\Theta(1/L).
    \label{eq:couplings_intro}
\end{align}
The claim is that if an excitation begins at site $j=1$, then the Hamiltonian evolution is such that at some fixed time $T_{\rm PST}= \Theta(L)$ it has deterministically arrived at site $L+1$:
\begin{align}
    e^{-iH_{\rm PST} T_{\rm PST}}\ket{100\ldots 000} = (-i)^L\ket{000\ldots 001}\,.
\end{align}
This technique has precedence for being used for other Hamiltonian constructions before. It is even used for lower bounds; a famous example is to show that simulating time evolution $e^{-iHt}$ with query access to $H$ requires $\Omega(\norm{H} t)$ queries in the worst-case \cite{Berry2007efficientSparse}. The way this is done is to encode the value of the parity function on $n$ bits in the output of simulating a norm one Hamiltonian $H$ simulated to time $\Theta(n)$. This is done using the perfect state transfer weighting, which gaurantees that after a fixed $\Theta(n)$ time, the output of $e^{-iHt}$ is \emph{exactly} the output of the parity function in a specified register. 
For us, this solves the ``overlap'' problem of Hamiltonian constructions. In standard clock constructions, the history state places only $1/(L+1)$ of its weight on the final step of the computation, preparing it as a ground state incurs polynomial overhead due to the $\Omega(1/L^2)$ spectral gap, and dynamics under uniform couplings disperses the wavepacket rather than delivering it to the end. Here, by contrast, the final step is reached with probability 1 after an evolution time linear in the path length.

  

\paragraph{QRAM Hamiltonian.} In the QRAM operation, we have an address $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ and a bus qubit $B$, and we want to load the bit $D_x$ at the address $x$ into $B$. It suffices to do this for a single address, by linearity. We will use the perfect state transfer trick for this, where it ensures fidelity 1 with the output state if it follows the path to the correct leaf. 

Perfect state transfer was designed to be applied to linear paths. Our construction navigates back and forth along a binary tree, as in \cref{fig:bucket-brigade}, rather than a linear path. The address $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ determines the sequence of steps along the tree. In the full proof, we formalize this as a directed acyclic graph consisting of many copies of the binary tree, where each $x$ maps to a path in the graph.  It is this path on which we are able to apply perfect state transfer and guarantee that the path is deterministically traversed in time proportional to the length of the path. Different values of $x$ lead to different paths, which route in order to pick up their respective bits $D_x$, but all paths have the same length and thus are completed deterministically at the same time.

In our construction, the relevant path length is $L = \Theta(\log^2(N))$---each step of the path corresponds to one time step in the sequence of configurations depicted in \cref{fig:bucket-brigade}. The length is quadratic because our construction requires placing the $\log N$ address bits at the appropriate nodes sequentially, going back to the root each time. Implementations of bucket-brigade in the circuit model are able to pipeline steps such that $O(\log N)$ depth is achieved \cite{HannNoise21}, but this technique is not obviously compatible with our construction. 

It remains to explain how  to ensure the right path is traversed, given an address setting $\ket{x}$. A key design choice of our construction is that all information is encoded in unary. That is, address states are encoded in pairs of qubits as $\ket{0} = \ket{\bullet \circ}$ and $\ket{1} = \ket{\circ \bullet}$, here adopting the notation we use in the full proof where each two level system is spanned by states $\ket{\circ}$ (unoccupied) and $\ket{\bullet}$ (occupied). For a particular address $x$, the initial state is just a configuration of $O(\log(N))$ excitations $\ket{\bullet}$, and all of the auxiliary qubits are asked to begin unoccupied in $\ket{\circ}$.  The path of length $L$ then corresponds to a sequence of changes to this initial configuration, where at most two excitations move from one register to another, in transitions such as
\begin{align}\label{eq:4-local}
\ket{\mathord{\bullet}~\mathord{\bullet}~\mathord{\circ}~\mathord{\circ}} \leftrightarrow \ket{\mathord{\circ}~\mathord{\circ}~\mathord{\bullet}~\mathord{\bullet}}\,.
\end{align}
We also require transitions where two excitations are combined into one or vice versa.
    \begin{align}\label{eq:3-local}
\ket{\bullet\bullet\circ} \leftrightarrow \ket{\circ\circ\bullet}\,.
\end{align}
In the more practical discussion of \cref{sec:experiment}, we discuss how here it is important for the outgoing excitation's inherent energy (e.g., the frequency of the transmon that realizes it) to be exactly twice the energy of two incoming excitations, so that energy is conserved. 

Each of these transitions corresponds to one of the perfect state transfer terms in \cref{eq:PST}, but its realization requires 4-local or 3-local interactions for \cref{eq:4-local} and \cref{eq:3-local}, respectively. This is why our construction has locality 4.

A basic implementation does not also achieve degree 4, because the address information deposited as an excitation at a particular intermediate node of the tree in \cref{fig:bucket-brigade} must then interact with many subsequent excitations descending to lower levels of the tree. Our solution to this is to introduce what we call the ``switch wire'' register at each binary tree node. This is a collection of qubits arranged in 1D---one 1D rail for $\ket{0}$ and one 1D rail for $\ket{1}$.   The deposited address information begins in the first slot or ``slice'' of this register. The first time this excitation interacts with another excitation, it advances to the second slot in the switch wire, and so forth. This prevents any individual slice from needing to interact with more than 4 other registers. This same trick is used in other aspects of our construction, as well, ensuring each configuration encountered along the path is unique and easily determined from the last by local logic, enforceable through perfect state transfer terms.  

\subsection{Noise resilience}
Now we address the issue of passively implementing the time-independent Hamiltonian.
The Hamiltonian acts on $\Theta(N)$ auxiliary qubits, so at first it seems that
one must prepare and protect all of them for every query. Fortunately, this is not true. The key point is that when we make a query on a given basis state $\ket{x}$ in the address register, the query is sensitive to  errors
only in a small part of the device. 

\paragraph{Branch isolation.}
Fix an address $x$.  During the ideal evolution, only
$F_n=\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(\log^2N)$ physical qubits can affect the root-to-leaf path for this address.
We call this set its \emph{footprint}. 
We show that in a formal sense, errors in disjoint pairs of footprints do not affect each other.
This is the continuous-time version of branch isolation for bucket-brigade QRAM~\cite{HannNoise21}.

Branch isolation is then used for all our noise bounds.
We never sum up the errors
over the full $\Theta(N)$ hardware, only the errors that affect the
branch being queried.

\paragraph{Thermal initialization and reuse.}
The physical Hamiltonian is $K=H+P$, where $P$ contains fixed on-site energy
penalties chosen so that $[H,P]=0$. We will use this Hamiltonian for our analysis of noise resilience. Let $\Delta$ be the gap between the vacant and excited states of a qubit, and let
$\kappa$ denote how much couplings can lower this energy.  The
effective gap is $g=\Delta-\kappa$.  At inverse temperature $\beta$, a fixed
footprint contains a defect with probability at most $F_ne^{-\beta g}$.

On the complementary event, the query is exact and returns the retained device
to the same state.
One can show that over $m$ queries,
\[
    \epsilon_m\le4m\sqrt{F_ne^{-\beta g}}.
\]
Hence
\[
    \beta g\ge\log F_n+2\log(4m/\varepsilon)
\]
suffices for error $\varepsilon$.  If $m,\varepsilon^{-1}=\poly(n)$ and
$g$ is constant, then $T=O(1/\log\log N)$. Hence we have to pay the cooling cost only once, and the temperature required scales inversely in $\log m$ for $m$ queries.  Each query uses only $O(n)$ root
operations, giving $O(\log N)$ energy per query. See \cref{sec:thermal} for details of the proof, and \cref{cor:boundary-energy} for a formal claim of the energy cost.

\paragraph{Persistent errors.}
To show that our construction is scalable, i.e. components only need to be implemented with $1/\polylog N$ precision, we bound the error due to imprecision in the Hamiltonian terms.  To show the bound, we compare the physical
device with the same noisy device that evolves \emph{idle} outside the branch being
queried.

For static imprecision, let $W$ be the largest total norm of perturbation terms
that can touch one branch.
Query $k$ can encounter damage accumulated during the first $k$ query
intervals.  Summing this accumulated damage gives
\[
    \epsilon_m\le2m(m+1)\tau W
      =O(m^2\lambda_{\rm err}\log^4N),
\]
where $\lambda_{\rm err}$ is the largest perturbation weight incident on one
physical qubit.

We can generalize this analysis to Markovian noise, modelled as a Lindbladian~\cite{Lindblad1976,GKS1976}. Let $G_j$ be the largest integrated noise exposure of one
branch during query $j$.  Tracking the amplitude for the noisy idle device to
return to its reference state gives
\[
    \epsilon_m
      \le8m\sum_{j=1}^m(m-j+1)G_j.
\]
If the incident noise rate on each qubit is at most $\gamma$, then
\[
    \epsilon_m=O(m^3\gamma\log^4N).
\]

See \cref{sec:imperfect,sec:dynamical} for detailed proofs. The important point is that every bound depends on the
$\Theta(\log^2N)$ branch footprint rather than on the full memory size.
For $m=\poly(n)$, the component precision is inverse-polynomial in $n=\log N$.

\section{The Hamiltonian}
\label{sec:hamiltonian}

The Hamiltonian has many terms. Each term is associated with an index $j=1,\ldots, L$, where $L$ is the ``schedule length''. The set of all terms associated with step $j$ are denoted $\mathcal{T}_j$, and all terms in $\mathcal{T}_j$ receive the same $j$-dependent weight designed to enforce perfect state transfer.  We write:
\begin{equation}
    H=\sum_{j=1}^{L} J_j\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_j}\left(T+T^\dagger\right).
\end{equation}
Where $J_j=\frac{\Omega}{2}\sqrt{j(L-j+1)}$, for $\Omega = \Theta(1/L)$. This equation is the decomposition used for the locality and degree bounds.  Each summand $J_j(T+T^\dagger)$ is Hermitian. The terms $T$ are described explicitly in \cref{sec:hamiltonian_terms}, but we first set up the notation in \cref{sec:notation}. There will be three kinds of terms: Exchange, Route, and Read. In addition to the address, bus, and memory qubits, these terms will act on the carrier and switch qubits.

\subsection{Evolution \& Notation}
\label{sec:notation}
In this section, we introduce the notation we need to specify the construction of the Hamiltonian. Everywhere below, single qubits encode whether a physical excitation is present in their mode as $\ket{\bullet}$ and its absence by $\ket{\circ}$. Registers will be comprised of 2 or 3 such qubits, and the configuration of excitations will record a value denoted by $\ket{\emptyset}, \ket{\star}, \ket{0}$ or $\ket{1}$.
Before giving the formal construction of the Hamiltonian it will be useful to concretize the description of its intended evolution, which follows the bucket-brigade QRAM circuit~\cite{GLL08}. We will be working over a complete binary tree of height $n$, with nodes $v\in\bits^{\le n}$, root $\mathcal{R} = \varnothing$.  The depth of $v$ is $|v|$.

Fix a computational-basis address \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\). The query has three stages. First, the carrier transports the address bits into switches along the branch specified by \(x\): bit \(x_k\) determines the direction taken at depth \(k-1\). Next, the carrier takes the bus value to leaf \(x\), reads the memory bit \(D_x\), and returns the updated value to the bus. Finally, it restores the address bits and empties the switches. This is visualized in \cref{fig:bucket-brigade}. We now describe the registers that implement this sequence. We first define the input and output registers, which are called address and bus.

\paragraph{Address and bus.}
The address registers $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ encode the input to the query. The query will eventually be read out from the bus register $B$. Each of them has three valid states, \begin{equation}
    \ket{\emptyset}=\ket{\circ\circ},\qquad
    \ket{0}=\ket{\bullet\circ},\qquad
    \ket{1}=\ket{\circ\bullet}.
\end{equation}

Now we will define the carrier and switch registers. The number of these depends on the evolution time of the Hamiltonian, so it will be useful to compute that first. The total evolution time is
\begin{equation}
    L = \sum_{k=1}^n 2k + (n+1) + 1 + (n+1) + \sum_{k=1}^n 2k = 2n^2+O(n)
    \label{eq:schedule-length}
\end{equation}
Loading $A_k$ takes $2k$ transitions: make the carrier bit, descend $k-1$ levels, store it, and return.  The query takes $2n+3$ transitions: absorb the bus value into the carrier, traverse to the leaf and read, return, and deposit the result back into $B$.  Unloading reverses the load, taking $2k$ transitions for bit $k$.

For $v$ at depth $d$, it is visited twice for each load, twice during the query, and twice for each unload. Let $R_v$ be the number of times $v$ is visited, then
\begin{equation}
    R_v = 2(n-d-1)+2+2(n-d-1)=4(n-d)-2,
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Carrier registers.}
We will have $O(N)$ carrier registers for many $(j,v)$ (step, node) pairs in the evolution. The carrier registers have 4 possible values. They can either be ``inactive" ($\ket \emptyset$) or ``active" and take the values $\ket{\star}, \ket{0}, \ket{1}$. Here we may imagine a register is active if it is occupied by a fermion or boson. Throughout the evolution we will maintain the invariant that there is a single active carrier register. This will be interpreted as the \emph{carrier} moving through the different nodes.

We encode each small register in unary. Every carrier register is realized by three qubits.  For every $j$ and every node $v$ in the binary tree such that $v$ could contain the carrier at step $j$, define the carrier register
\begin{equation}
    \car_{j,v}=(q^\star_{j,v},q^0_{j,v},q^1_{j,v}).
\end{equation}
The valid states of one register are
\begin{equation}
    \ket{\emptyset}=\ket{\circ\circ\circ},\qquad
    \ket\star=\ket{\bullet\circ\circ},\qquad
    \ket{0}=\ket{\circ\bullet\circ},\qquad
    \ket{1}=\ket{\circ\circ\bullet}.
\end{equation}
A valid history state has exactly one active carrier register across all layers and sites.  Initially this carrier is $\ket\star$ at the root. The active carrier register plays a dual role. Its position acts as a clock, tracking the step of the evolution. And its state encodes for example whether there is an address bit currently being routed, and if so what is its value.

\paragraph{Switch wires.}
For each internal node $v\in\bits^{<n}$ recall that $R_v=4(n-|v|) - 2$. This number is how many times the carrier will visit this node on a valid evolution of the Hamiltonian if $v$ lies on the branch of the tree corresponding to the query. Define a sequence of \emph{switch wire} registers

\begin{equation}
    Y_{v,0},Y_{v,1},\ldots,Y_{v,R_v},
    \qquad
    Y_{v,r}=(q^0_{v,r},q^1_{v,r}),
\end{equation}
with valid states
\begin{equation}
    \ket{\emptyset}=\ket{\circ\circ},\qquad
    \ket{0}=\ket{\bullet\circ},\qquad
    \ket{1}=\ket{\circ\bullet}.
\end{equation}
All switch registers are initialized to $\ket{\emptyset}$. The value \(c\in\{0,1\}\) is encoded by an excitation in qubit \(q^c\). When node $v$ stores the address bit $a_{|v|+1}$, the excitation starts in qubit $Y_{v,0}$ and advances from $Y_{v,i-1}$ to $Y_{v, i}$ each time $v$ is acted on by a Hamiltonian term. Unrolling the counter of how many times this node has been visited into many registers encoded in unary is what keeps the interaction hypergraph degree 4.

\paragraph{Schedule DAG.}
The schedule records the carrier's position after each elementary
operation. At each step, the carrier either stays at the same tree node,
moves to a child, or moves to its parent. The order of these operations
and their depths are fixed independently of the input address.

We represent the schedule by a layered directed acyclic graph (DAG) with
layers
\[
    U_j=\{(j,v):v\text{ is a possible carrier position after step }j\},
    \qquad j=0,\ldots,L.
\]
Vertex $(j,v)$ corresponds to the carrier register $\car_{j,v}$.
Every edge goes from layer $j-1$ to layer $j$. Depending on the
scheduled operation, the edges have one of three forms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
    (j-1,v)&\longrightarrow(j,v)
        &&\text{stay at the same tree node},\\
    (j-1,v)&\longrightarrow(j,vc)
        &&\text{move to child }vc, ~c\in\bits,\\
    (j-1,vc)&\longrightarrow(j,v)
        &&\text{move to the parent}.
\end{aligned}
\]
At each step we include all edges of the prescribed form at the
prescribed depth. Even an operation that stays at the same tree node
moves between distinct carrier registers, since the layer changes.
The local terms defined below specify how each transition changes
the values held by the registers.

For a basis address $x$, the schedule and the directions specified
by $x$ determine a branch walk
\[
    u_0(x),\ldots,u_L(x),
    \qquad u_j(x)=(j,v_j(x)),
\]
starting at $(0,\mathcal R)$.
When we define the terms in \cref{sec:hamiltonian_terms}, $\car_s$ and $\car_t$ 
will denote the source and target carrier registers of the edge under discussion.

\paragraph{Memory.}
For each leaf $x\in\bits^n$ there is a memory qubit $M_x$, initialized as $\ket{D_x}$.  The Hamiltonian acts diagonally on memory and never changes $D$. Since this qubit only needs to store classical data, we can imagine these registers as classical memory and will not worry about their initialization or coherence.

\paragraph{Elementary operators.}
We will define the operators which will help us define the Hamiltonian in \cref{sec:hamiltonian_terms}, and we will use the fact that we encoded our states in unary. Each register is a block of qubits (a carrier register is the three qubits
$q^\star,q^0,q^1$; a switch slice is the two qubits $q^0,q^1$), and every term of the
Hamiltonian is a product of single-qubit ladder operators, one per qubit it touches. On a
single qubit, $\sgp=\lvert\bullet\rangle\!\langle\circ\rvert$ raises and $\sgm=\lvert\circ\rangle\!\langle\bullet\rvert$
lowers. In other words, $\sgp$ creates an excitation and $\sgm$ removes one, with $\sgp\ket\bullet=0$ and
$\sgm\ket\circ=0$. We address an individual qubit by its register and its value: for a register
$R$ and a value $c$ in $R$'s alphabet, write
\begin{equation}
  \cre{R}{c}\ \text{and}\ \ann{R}{c}
  \qquad\text{for }\sgp\ \text{and}\ \sgm\ \text{on the qubit }q^c\text{ of }R,
  \label{eq:op-dictionary}
\end{equation}
so $\cre{R}{c}$ writes value $c$ into $R$ and $\ann{R}{c}$ removes it. Relabeling
a register from value $c'$ to $c$ is then the product $\cre{R}{c}\ann{R}{c'}$, since the unary
encoding stores the value in which qubit is up. A term fires only when its lowering operators meet
occupied (active) qubits.

\subsection{Construction}
\label{sec:hamiltonian_terms}

Now we recall the weights needed to construct a perfect state transfer Hamiltonian with evolution time $L$,
\begin{equation}
    J_j=\frac{\Omega}{2}\sqrt{j(L-j+1)},
    \qquad
    \Omega=\Theta(1/L).
    \label{eq:couplings}
\end{equation}
For each layer $j$ there is a set $\mathcal T_j$ of terms at step $j$ if the schedule.
Recall that the Hamiltonian is
\begin{equation}
    H=\sum_{j=1}^{L} J_j\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_j}\left(T+T^\dagger\right).
    \label{eq:H}
\end{equation}
The source and target carrier registers are those of the corresponding edge in the layered graph we defined in the previous subsection. They are denoted by $\car_s$ and $\car_t$ inside the local formulas.

There are only three kinds of terms: exchange a bit with the carrier,
route through a switch, and read a memory bit.

\paragraph{Exchange a bit with the carrier.}
Let $R$ be any register with states
$\ket\emptyset,\ket0,\ket1$.  An exchange layer moves one bit between $R$
and the carrier:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
    \mathcal T_j
      &=\left\{
        \cre{\car_t}{c}\ann{\car_s}{\star}\ann{R}{c}:c\in\bits
      \right\},
      &&\text{if the bit moves from $R$ to the carrier},\\
    \mathcal T_j
      &=\left\{
        \cre{\car_t}{\star}\ann{\car_s}{c}\cre{R}{c}:c\in\bits
      \right\},
      &&\text{if the bit moves from the carrier to $R$}.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:carrier-exchange}
\end{equation}
On valid states these are the two directions of
\[
    \ket\star_{\car_s}\ket c_R
      \longleftrightarrow
    \ket c_{\car_t}\ket\emptyset_R.
\]

We use this same interaction on three kinds of registers.  At the root, an
address bit is transferred from $A_k$ into the carrier before it is routed,
and returned to $A_k$ after that part of the schedule is reversed.  At a tree
node, the carrier transfers the address bit into the first slice $Y_{v,0}$ of
the switch wire; after the later routing steps have advanced that excitation
to $Y_{v,R_v}$, the carrier takes it back.  Finally, the bus value is
transferred into the carrier before the leaf traversal and returned to $B$
after the carrier comes back to the root.  Thus all three uses are the same
three-local interaction.

\paragraph{Route through a switch.}
At a routing layer $j$, let $S_j\subseteq\{\star,0,1\}$ be the carrier values
that can occur on a valid history.  Thus $S_j=\{\star\}$ when the carrier
holds no bit and $S_j=\{0,1\}$ when it carries an address or bus bit.  In
particular, $|S_j|\le2$.

Suppose the layer routes through depth $d$.  For $v\in\bits^d$, let
$r=r_j(v)$ be the active switch slice.  For each child $b\in\bits$ and
$s\in S_j$, include
\begin{equation}
    R_{v,r,b,s}
      =\cre{\car_t}{s}\ann{\car_s}{s}
       \ann{Y_{v,r}}{b}\cre{Y_{v,r+1}}{b},
    \qquad
    \mathcal T_j
      =\{R_{v,r_j(v),b,s}:v\in\bits^d,\ b\in\bits,\ s\in S_j\}.
    \label{eq:route}
\end{equation}
For a downward route the carrier edge is $v\to vb$; for an upward route it is
$vb\to v$.  The term moves the carrier along the child selected by the stored
bit and advances that switch excitation by one slice.  The wrong-child term

- A circuit-to-Hamiltonian construction that avoids the usual clock pathologies: output fidelity 1 at a *prescribed* time $O(n^2)$, not $1/L$ overlap with a history state.

\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We show that if quantum commitments exist, then either there is no polynomial-time solution to the unitary synthesis problem, or $\mathsf{BPP} \neq \mathsf{NEXP}$.
Thus, showing unconditionally that quantum commitments exist would require answering at least one of two longstanding open questions in complexity theory.
We prove our main result as a consequence of a more general lemma, which shows that every unitary in $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ either cannot be synthesized efficiently relative to any classical oracle, or can be synthesized efficiently with an oracle for $\mathsf{NEXP}$ search problems.
Our lemma has other noteworthy consequences, including that certain oracle separations involving $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ would imply breakthrough classical lower bounds such as $\mathsf{NC} \neq \mathsf{NP}$.

Along the way, we propose new definitions for the unitary complexity classes $\mathsf{unitaryP}$ and $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$.
Our changes address the biggest conceptual issues with definitions suggested in prior work, and lead to elegant proofs.
We study both implementations that erase garbage and implementations that allow it, because we cannot rule out the possibility that the two definitions differ.
Nevertheless, we show that both definitions can be viewed as special cases of each other.
We also showcase many other ways in which our definitions are robust.
For example, we show that $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ has an equivalent characterization as the set of unitary transformations whose entries can be computed to arbitrary precision in polynomial space.
Consequently, we deduce that $\mathsf{unitaryPSPACE}$ can generically erase garbage, a result that provably fails relative to unitary oracles.
\end{abstract}
