\section{Introduction}

The complexity of quantum-input computational tasks may behave radically different than the intuitions we have from classical computation.
For example, a basic principle in classical cryptography is that all superpolynomially-computationally secure cryptosystems rely on the hardness assumption $\P \neq \NP$, with few exceptions.
Yet, several works~\cite{Kre21-pseudorandom,KQST23-prs,KQT24-owf} have established that the same might not be true of \textit{quantum} cryptography, by constructing oracles relative to which $\NP$-complete problems are easy and yet nontrivial quantum cryptography exists.

Motivated by these separations, a flurry of work has attempted to characterize the world of cryptography that could exist without assuming $\P \neq \NP$, now regularly called ``Microcrypt''~\cite{Sat26-zoo}.
A large fraction of this effort has gone toward identifying the \textit{minimal} primitive that is necessary for quantum cryptography, much the same way that one-way functions are considered the foundation without which classical cryptography could not exist~\cite{IL89-owf,Imp95-average}.
Quantum commitment schemes have emerged as the most promising such candidate, as they have many equivalent notions and are implied by almost all other forms of quantum cryptography~\cite{Yan22-commitments,BCQ23-efi,HMY23-superpositions,KT24-commitments,BJ24-commitments,CCC+26-meta}.

The complexity-theoretic picture surrounding quantum commitments is particularly perplexing: commitments are not known to imply \textit{any} kind of hardness or separation in standard complexity theory.
In fact, some researchers are optimistic that the existence of quantum commitments might not be subject to the same barriers of relativization~\cite{BGS75-p-np}, natural proofs~\cite{RR97-nat-proofs}, or algebrization~\cite{AW09-algebrization} that have thus far prevented attacks on the $\P \stackrel{?}{=} \NP$ problem.
It is conceivable that we could unconditionally prove the computational security of a quantum commitment scheme, using only the complexity-theoretic lower bound techniques that we know of today.
Indeed, \cite{Qia24-unconditional,MNY24-unconditional} recently demonstrated this possibility in the \textit{auxiliary input model}, in which all parties receive copies of a (possibly exponentially-complex) advice state on a polynomial number of qubits.

So, does traditional complexity theory have \textit{nothing} to say about the hardness that underlies quantum cryptography?
Or, is there some yet-unknown method to show that quantum cryptography would still imply breakthrough classical lower bounds?
This uncertainty is best captured in the unresolved \textit{unitary synthesis problem}~\cite{AK07-qcma-qma,Ros21-unitary,LMW24-synthesis}.
First posed over 20 years ago, it asks whether unitary computation always reduces efficiently to classical computation.
More formally, a positive resolution to unitary synthesis means the existence of a $\poly(n)$-time quantum oracle algorithm such that for every $n$-qubit unitary transformation $U$, there exists a choice of the classical oracle function that allows the algorithm to approximately implement $U$.
An efficient unitary synthesis algorithm, then, would at least show that any superpolynomial lower bounds for a unitary implementation problem would yield superpolynomial hardness of \textit{some} classical function.

Still, it is not clear whether unitary synthesis ought to directly inform quantum cryptography or vice versa.
For one, the unitary synthesis problem as originally stated is purely existential; it says nothing about how the oracle function's complexity relates to the unitary $U$!
Conversely, even a negative solution to unitary synthesis could be highly nonexplicit.
A lower bound for synthesizing Haar-random unitaries $U$ might not be directly relevant to the hardness of any particular quantum commitment scheme.

The hope of using quantum states as a new foundation for cryptography and the lack of a clear connection to classical complexity theory have motivated the introduction of a ``quantum-native'' language of complexity theory that treats quantum transformations as first-class objects.
Whereas ordinary complexity classes such as $\P$, $\BQP$, or $\PSPACE$ capture classical-input decision problems, some newly-defined classes express \textit{unitary transformation} problems, where the computational task is to coherently apply a quantum operation on an unknown and arbitrary input state~\cite{RY22,MY23,BEMPQY26-uhlmann,Zha25-unitary-oracles}.
Two obvious choices for classes to study are $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$, which correspond to the unitary transformations that can be implemented in polynomial time or space, respectively, on a quantum computer.
We defer a formal treatment of the definitions until \Cref{sec:detour}.
For now, we note that the $\uP \stackrel{?}{=} \uPSPACE$ problem has already emerged as a central question in the context of cryptography, because it has been shown that the existence of any falsifiable computationally-secure quantum cryptosystem implies the separation $\uP \neq \uPSPACE$~\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann}.
Thus, while we do not know whether the existence of quantum commitments would (say) imply a separation of $\P$ and $\PSPACE$, they would at least separate $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$.

\subsection{This work}
\label{sec:this_work}

Broadly speaking, the first goal of this paper is to probe the computational hardness of $\uPSPACE$ using classical complexity-theoretic techniques.
For example, our most easily-stated result establishes a direct connection between quantum cryptography, the unitary synthesis problem, and classical lower bounds:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{cor:efi_bpp_nexp}, informal]
    \label{thm:main-informal}
    Suppose quantum commitments exist.
    Then either:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item There is no polynomial-time solution to the unitary synthesis problem, or
        \item $\BPP \neq \NEXP$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

Recall that $\BPP$ is the set of problems solvable in randomized polynomial time, while $\NEXP$ is nondeterministic \textit{exponential} time.
Some might be surprised to find that $\BPP \stackrel{?}{=} \NEXP$ is a question that we do not yet know the answer to, but it has been open ever since the classes were first defined and remains one of the frontier questions in classical complexity theory.
Consequently, any unconditional proof that quantum commitments exist would have to resolve at least one of a 20+ year old open problem~\cite{AK07-qcma-qma} or a 40+ year old one~\cite{Hel86-bpp-exp,BFL91-mip-nexp}!

We prove \Cref{thm:main-informal} as a consequence of the following key lemma, stated in terms of unitary complexity classes:

\begin{restatable}[\Cref{lem:unitarypspace_dichotomy_witnexp}, informal]{lemma}{lemintrokey}
    \label{lem:all-fnexp-informal}
    For every $\calU \in \uPSPACE$, either
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\calU \not\in \uP^\ALL$, or
        \item $\calU \in \uP^\FNEXP$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{restatable}

Here, $\uP^\class{K}$ is the set of unitary problems that can be solved in polynomial time with an oracle from $\class{K}$, and $\ALL$ is the set of all languages.
Thus, $\uP^\ALL$ is shorthand for the set of unitaries that \textit{do} admit an efficient unitary synthesis algorithm relative to some oracle.
(Indeed, in the above notation, one can express the unitary synthesis problem succinctly as $\uP^\ALL \stackrel{?}{=} \uALL$, where $\uALL$ is the set of all unitaries.)
For the second item, $\FNEXP$ denotes the set of $\NEXP$ search problems, and an oracle for $\FNEXP$ means the ability to query the bits of some valid $\NEXP$ witness (see \Cref{sec:nexp_relations} for more details).
Hence, \Cref{lem:all-fnexp-informal} shows that for every unitary $\calU$ implementable in polynomial space, either $\calU$ is ``unitary synthesis-hard'' in the sense that it cannot be implemented efficiently relative to any classical oracle, or $\calU$ reduces efficiently to $\NEXP$ witness search.

Lombardi, Ma, and Wright~\cite{LMW24-synthesis} once remarked that we do not even know whether an oracle for the \textit{halting problem} suffices to break every quantum commitment scheme, or more generally to synthesize unitaries in $\uPSPACE$.
While true, \Cref{lem:all-fnexp-informal} shows that that statement is perhaps misleading, as for every unitary in $\uPSPACE$, either a halting oracle is as useless as any other, or it is substantial overkill.

Another way to interpret \Cref{lem:all-fnexp-informal} is as a statement that a positive resolution to unitary synthesis would immediately place an upper bound on the power of an oracle needed to implement $\uPSPACE$ efficiently:

\begin{corollary}[\Cref{cor:u-all-up-all}, informal]
    \label{cor:upspace_fnexp}
    If $\uALL = \uP^\ALL$, then $\uPSPACE \subseteq \uP^\FNEXP$.
\end{corollary}

\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} raised the question of how unitary complexity classes formally relate to their classical counterparts.
As one concrete example, they asked: does $\P = \PSPACE$ imply $\uP = \uPSPACE$, or can one give oracle evidence that it does not?
More generally, one could also ask about a ``$\PSPACE$-effective'' version of unitary synthesis: $\uPSPACE \stackrel{?}{=} \uP^\PSPACE$.
Indeed, if polynomial-space unitaries \textit{can} be synthesized efficiently, it is natural to want the classical oracle to also be computable in polynomial space.
Assuming the unitary synthesis conjecture, \cref{cor:upspace_fnexp} almost obtains ``$\PSPACE$-effective'' synthesis, but with the $\PSPACE$ oracle replaced by $\FNEXP$.
Nevertheless, we emphasize that $\FNEXP$ is not known to be separated from $\PSPACE$.
For example, if $\AM = \NEXP$, then the $\FNEXP$ oracle can be replaced by $\PSPACE$ as a consequence of the \textit{easy witness lemma} of Impagliazzo, Kabanets, and Wigderson~\cite{IKW02-easy-witness}.
Thus \cref{cor:upspace_fnexp} gives a condition under which $\PSPACE$-effective unitary synthesis reduces to full unitary synthesis.
Or, stated another way, we have:

\begin{corollary}[\Cref{cor:nc_np_separation}, informal]
    \label{cor:am_nexp_informal}
    If $\uP^{\PSPACE} \neq \uPSPACE$, then at least one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\uP^{\ALL} \neq \uALL$, or
        \item $\AM \neq \NEXP$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

We remark that most of our results relativize in some fashion, and in the formal statements of our results, we will always be completely explicit about how the statements hold relative to oracles.
In one case, we even show that \textit{a mere oracle separation} involving $\uPSPACE$ would imply new non-oracular lower bounds:

\begin{corollary}[\Cref{cor:nc_np_separation}, informal]
    \label{cor:nc_np_informal}
    If there is a language $L$ relative to which $\uP^{\PSPACE^L} \neq \uPSPACE^{L}$, then either
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\uP^{\ALL} \neq \uALL$, or
        \item $\NC \neq \NP$
    \end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

Here, $\NC$ is the set of problems solvable in polylogarithmic time on a machine with a polynomial number of parallel processors.
Like most complexity separations, whether $\NC \stackrel{?}{=} \NP$ is wide open, and we emphasize that the second implication does \textit{not} involve relativization.
This is noteworthy because \cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} left open the problem of constructing a classical oracle $L$ relative to which $\P^L = \PSPACE^L$ but $\uP^L \neq \uPSPACE^L$.
\Cref{cor:nc_np_separation} explains why such an oracle has remained elusive: it would either have to resolve the unitary synthesis problem, or yield a breakthrough lower bound in classical complexity!

\section{Detour: (re)defining unitary complexity classes}
\label{sec:detour}

It has proven challenging to settle upon good definitions of unitary complexity classes, in part because they behave less robustly than traditional complexity classes such as $\P$ or $\BQP$.
Indeed, there are many reasonable-looking choices one can make in the definitions that lead to starkly different notions.
As one example, unitary complexity classes are typically defined allowing some kind of error in the implementation, not just because we want to capture probabilistic algorithms, but also because often the gates in a quantum circuit are discrete even though the unitary families we want to implement are continuous.
Yet unlike with (say) $\BQP$, there is no generic method for error \textit{reduction}: the standard technique of amplifying a Monte Carlo algorithm by repetition plus majority voting has no analogue in the unitary setting.
So, unitary complexity classes must make a choice for how to bake error reduction into the definition.
The many possible choices have led to numerous different definitions for the complexity classes $\uP$ (often denoted $\class{unitaryBQP}$\footnote{We find it strange and inconsistent that the ``$\class{BQ}$'' prefix typically makes its way into $\class{unitaryBQP}$ but not $\uPSPACE$. As the ``$\class{Q}$'' meaning ``quantum'' is made redundant by ``$\class{unitary}$,'' we prefer the more succinct notation.}) and $\uPSPACE$~\cite{RY22,MY23,BEMPQY26-uhlmann,Zha25-unitary-oracles}.

\subsection{Why do we need new definitions?}

Despite the variety of definitions for unitary complexity classes, all existing proposals present serious issues.
Disconcertingly, it is not clear whether the results claimed in these works are insensitive to the selections made in their respective definitions.
If we wish to put unitary complexity on solid foundations, we have to ensure that the definitions that we choose are sensible.
We now describe the most critical issues with prior definitions: these involve showing that one can ``smuggle'' a hard-to-compute unitary into a class which intuitively should not capture such a problem.

Rosenthal and Yuen~\cite{RY22} and Metger and Yuen~\cite{MY23} were some of the earliest works to study unitary complexity, but the first formal treatment of unitary complexity classes was defined and investigated in the work of Bostanci, Efron, Metger, Poremba, Qian, and Yuen~\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann}.
The central trouble with their definition is with how it treats error: an $n$-qubit unitary is in $\uP$ as defined by them, when there is a circuit of size $\poly(n, 1/\eps)$ which approximates the unitary to $\eps$ error.\footnote{The arXiv v1 version of \cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} used a different definition with further issues that were discovered by the first author, Fermi Ma, and John Wright, and subsequently raised to the authors.
The arXiv v3 of their preprint details these objections, responds, and made changes to address some of them.
The class as discussed here is based on their most recent definition.}
This definition is self-consistent until we introduce a notion of $\uPSPACE$, which is defined analogously, except that the circuit must merely use space $\poly(n, 1/\eps)$.
At this point, we can try composing different unitary complexity classes: for example, we expect that $\uPSPACE$ is not strengthened when we provide it with a $\uP$ oracle; in other words, we expect that $\uPSPACE^\uP = \uPSPACE$, as is true for the non-unitary versions of these classes.
More generally, we should even expect that $\uPSPACE$ is self-low, meaning $\uPSPACE^\uPSPACE = \uPSPACE$.
However, this is not the case under the conventional notion of oracle access: consider the task of, given an $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, applying the unitary
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:u_x_exp}
    U_x = \begin{bmatrix}
        1 \\ & e^{\ii \pi L(x) / 2^n}
    \end{bmatrix},
\end{equation}
where $L(x)$ is a function which requires exponential time and space to compute.
Then this unitary is in their $\uP$, as it is close to the identity for large $\eps$, and the phase can be computed in $\poly(1/\eps)$ time for $\eps$ exponentially small in $n$.
However, if we give a polynomial-space circuit access to $U_x$, it can compute $U_x^{2^n} = Z^{L(x)}$ and therefore implement a unitary which requires exponential space.

\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} handles this corner case by switching to an extremely non-standard notion of oracle access: they specify that, when a class is given an oracle, the resulting circuit must satisfy the error guarantee, even when the oracle is replaced with \emph{an adversarially chosen perturbation of the oracle}.
Encoding robustness into the notion of the oracle is an unnecessary concession: if instead we required the time/space complexities to scale polynomially with $\log(1/\eps)$ instead of $1/\eps$, this issue does not arise, and the statement $\uPSPACE^\uP = \uPSPACE$ holds for the conventional notion of oracle.
However, the authors settle for these infelicities, as their main results critically rely on the more generous error scaling of their definitions.

The other prominent suite of definitions were proposed by Zhandry~\cite{Zha25-unitary-oracles}.
Zhandry points out that having complexity scale inverse polynomially with error is unsuitable for cryptographic applications, and proposes three alternative definitions of $\uP$/$\uPSPACE$, where a circuit for implementing $U$ is required to have either arbitrarily-small inverse-polynomial, negligible, or arbitrarily-small inverse-exponential error in $n$.
Curiously, the dependence on the error scaling is handled in a non-uniform manner, meaning that the length of source code describing a quantum algorithm could blow up arbitrarily between (say) $\eps = 1/n$ to $\eps = 1/{2n}$.
Though, inverse-exponential error does address some of the issues of the prior work.
However, having error scale with $n$ (as opposed to being a parameter which one can choose independently) again leads to issues under composition.
As before, we can hide a difficult problem in a slight phase, such that it can be implemented to inverse-exponential error, but when this is given as an oracle to a more powerful class which can apply it repeatedly, the difficult problem is revealed.
Consider the example of, given $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, applying
\begin{equation*}
    U_x = \begin{bmatrix}
        1 \\ & e^{\ii \pi L(x) / 2^{2^n}}
    \end{bmatrix},
\end{equation*}
but now let $L(x)$ be an undecidable function, such as the halting problem.
Then the identity implements $U_x$ to any inverse-exponential error $\eps = 2^{-\poly(n)}$.
However, a polynomial-time algorithm given the padded input $x | 1^{2^{2^{|x|}}}$ can use an oracle for $U_x$ to compute $U_x^{2^{2^n}} = Z^{L(x)}$, and thus solves an undecidable problem.
The failure of ``closure under padding'' is resolved by requiring the existence of an efficient circuit for all $\eps$, not just for $\eps$ with a particular scaling in $n$.

\subsection{Motivating our definitions}

We wanted to ensure that our results rest on rigorous footing, rather than leaving any possibility that they are the consequences of arbitrary choices.
As such, we consider it essential to derive a set of unitary complexity definitions forward from first principles instead of backward from results.
We posit that a good complexity class should satisfy several properties:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Robust:} the class should remain the same, even if the definition is altered slightly, or the underlying implementation details are changed.
    \item \textbf{Consistent:} definitions should follow a common pattern across similar classes.
    \item \textbf{Intuitive:} the class should behave consistently with our intuition about the types of computations we are trying to capture.
    For example, it should include the kinds of problems which we expect it to include.
    \item \textbf{Composable:} fundamental ``composition'' operations like oracle reductions should be natural and produce sensible outcomes.
\end{enumerate}

These desiderata will guide us as we make our definitions.
We will discuss the reasoning behind how we make our choices, and point out when our choices (1) are cosmetic, so a different choice would produce the same class; (2) lead to materially different but reasonable classes; or (3) are critical to making well-behaved classes.

In this work, we consider $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$, which ought to have the following colloquial definition.

\begin{center}
    $\uP$/$\uPSPACE$ is the class of \textit{unitary languages} which \\ can be \textit{implemented} in \textit{polynomial time/space} on a \textit{quantum computer}.
\end{center}

We now formalize this definition, piece by piece.

\paragraph{``unitary language'':}
For us, a unitary problem is a sequence of unitaries of increasing size, $\{U_n\}_{n \in \N}$ where $U_n$ is a unitary on $n$ qubits (\cref{def:u-language}).
This sequence of unitaries can be thought of as defining a problem for every input size, where the problem is to apply the appropriate unitary to the input state.
For example, one might define the unitary language \textsc{QFT} of applying the $n$-qubit quantum Fourier transform.

Previous works~\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann,Zha25-unitary-oracles} define unitary problems differently: they index their unitaries by strings $x \in \{0,1\}^*$.
This does not affect the expressivity of unitary languages.
Languages in our sense can be converted to languages in their sense by taking $U_x = U_{\abs{x}}$, and languages in their sense can be converted into languages in our sense by defining $U_{2n}$ to be the unitary which takes $\ket{x}\ket{\psi}$ to $\ket{x} U_x \ket{\psi}$.
However, it is often useful to apply the unitary to a coherent superposition of inputs $x$, which makes the latter notion more convenient.

\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} also allow their implementation problems to consist of \textit{partial isometries}, which only need to implement a given unitary on some promised subspace.
Hence, partial isometries generalize unitary transformations in the same way that promise problems generalize languages.
While it would be interesting to generalize our definitions in the same fashion, we choose to focus on the conceptually simplest case.

Because we choose to only index by input size, we do not have a hard-coded classical input to our problems.
Note that we cannot make our choice simpler by discarding the index over $n$, since we need to apply a different map for different input sizes.

\paragraph{``implemented'':}
Here, we make two different choices about how to formalize this.
For us, to implement a unitary $U_n$ is to be able to, for every $\eps$, find a unitary quantum circuit $C_{n, \eps}$ such that, for all $n$-qubit states $\ket{\psi}$, one of the following two conditions holds:
\begin{align*}
    C_{n,\eps}(\ket{\psi}\ket{0^a}) &\approx_\eps (U\ket{\psi}) \ket{0^a} \\
    C_{n,\eps}(\ket{\psi}\ket{0^a}) &\approx_\eps (U\ket{\psi}) \ket{g} \text{ for some } \ket{g} \text{ independent of } \ket{\psi}
\end{align*}
The first definition requires that our implementation return the ancilla qubits to their initial state; the second is not concerned with this choice, and asks only that $U$ be correctly applied to the first register.
We refer to the resulting classes as $\uP/\uPSPACE$ and $\puP$/$\puPSPACE$, respectively.
Note that the first definition maintains global phase information on $U$, but the second definition allows the circuit to implement $U$ with any global phase, because the phase can be viewed as part of the garbage state $\ket{g}$.
The forgetting of global phase is the sense in which $\puP$ is ``projective,'' referring to the projective unitary group of unitary matrices modulo phase.
However, it is not \textit{a priori} clear whether the two definitions produce the same class after disregarding global phase.

The choice between allowing or disallowing garbage was the most contentious topic among the authors of this paper.
Both appear to be valid choices, both could be argued to capture the notion of ``implementing'' a unitary, and both have precedent in prior work, with \cite{Zha25-unitary-oracles} using the clean notion and \cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} allowing garbage.
The garbage-free definition has the advantage that it is, well, \textit{cleaner}.
And even though global phase is unobservable, it is often convenient to keep track of it in quantum algorithms, e.g.\ in linear combinations of unitaries~\cite{cw12}.
Certain operations, such as mapping $U$ to its controlled operation $\controlled U$, only make sense when the global phase is defined.
Zhandry uses precisely these arguments to favor $\uP$ over $\puP$, but we chose to include both, for three reasons.
First, we find it hard to deny that implementing a unitary with garbage should count as implementing that unitary.
Second, we cannot rule out that the set of unitaries which can be implemented efficiently with garbage is substantively larger than those which can be implemented cleanly.
(In fact, we show that relative to unitary oracles, allowing implementations with garbage yields \textit{strictly more} power; see \Cref{thm:no_global_phase_informal} further below.)
Finally, provided that we generally only work with $\puP$ modulo the global phase, there are no complexity-theoretic inconsistencies.

A naive choice would be to not allow any error, and instead require an exact implementation of $U_n$ (as if we took $\eps = 0$ above).
However, this would mean that changing the underlying gate set used in the quantum computer would yield different definitions of $\uP$.
So, we allow some error in implementation.

On the other hand, the choice of error metric turns out not to matter.
Up to polynomial overhead, the definitions above are equivalent to other sensible definitions.
In particular, the clean definition is equivalent to requiring that $C_{n, \eps}$ is close to an \emph{extension} of $U$ (i.e., some $\overline{U}$ such that $\overline{U} \ket{\psi} \ket{0^a} = (U \ket{\psi}) \ket{0^a}$) in operator norm.
The garbage definition is equivalent to requiring that $C_{n, \eps}$ is close to a \emph{dilation} of $U$ (i.e., some $\overline{U}$ such that $\overline{U} \ket{\psi} \ket{0^a} = (U \ket{\psi}) \ket{g}$) in diamond norm or operator norm.
It is also equivalent to requiring that $C_{n, \eps}$ is close to $U$ in diamond norm upon tracing out the ancilla register.
Note that these are all notions of \emph{worst-case} error, where we would like to be close for all inputs.

Technically, our earlier choice to index by length $n$ rather than strings $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ could materially affect the definitions of $\puP$ and $\puPSPACE$, as the ability to implement the map $\ket{\psi} \to U_x\ket{\psi}$ individually for every $x$ might not let us coherently apply the map $\ket{x}\ket{\psi} \to \ket{x}U_x\ket{\psi}$ on a superposition over $x$; the latter requires that the same garbage state is produced for every $\ket{x}$.
Indeed, \cite[Section 3.6.1]{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} raises the same concern and uses it to argue for indexing by classical input strings.
However, it turns out that even if different $x$ yield different garbage states, there is a different way that we can coherently encode all of the unitaries $U_x$ into a single larger unitary.
Namely, one can coherently apply the map $\ket{x}\ket{\psi}\ket{\phi} \to \ket{x}U_x\ket{\psi}U_x^\dagger\ket{\phi}$ (a consequence of \Cref{thm:garbage_iff_informal}).

\paragraph{``polynomial time/space'':}

We require that our algorithms run in time/space polynomial in $n$, the input size, as well as $\log 1/\eps$.
This differs from the choice of~\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann}, which only requires polynomial time/space in $n$ and $1/\eps$.
Zhandry is agnostic to this choice, making three different classes according to the scaling of $\eps$ as a fixed function of $n$.

Another difference here compared to prior work is to require \textit{uniform} dependence on both $n$ and $\eps$: we assume the existence of a polynomial-time/space Turing machine $M$ such that $M(1^n, \eps)$ outputs a description of a quantum circuit $C_{n, \eps}$ with the desired guarantee.
The Turing machine has a write-only output tape that specifies $C_{n, \eps}$ one gate at a time; this allows a polynomial-space machine to specify an exponentially-long circuit, so long as the circuit uses only a polynomial number of qubits.

The choices of error dependence are the subject of the greatest disagreement among different definitions: \cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} uses polynomial scaling with $\eps$ as a uniform parameter, while \cite{Zha25-unitary-oracles} argues for negligible or inverse-exponential error with circuits only specified for $\eps$ scaling with a fixed function of $n$, non-uniformly.
Our choice of scaling is the only option that leads to well-behaved definitions.
As mentioned before, choosing a larger scaling than $\polylog(1/\eps)$ runs into issues with composition.
In particular, self-lowness of $\uPSPACE$ fails if the allowed runtime is $s(\log 1/\eps)$ for some superpolynomial $s$, by considering the same $U_x$ from \Cref{eq:u_x_exp} but with $L(x)$ a hard language for space $s(n)$.
On the other hand, if the error scaling were \textit{smaller} than $\log(1/\eps)$, then $\uP$ would no longer be robust to changing the gate set, as the Solovay--Kitaev theorem requires $\Omega(\log 1/\eps)$ gates to compile an arbitrary quantum gate into a universal gate set.
Additionally, if $\eps$ scales with $n$ and cannot be scaled arbitrarily, then self-lowness fails again, and the complexity class is no longer closed under padding: problems become \textit{harder} when they are padded, an unintuitive outcome.

\cite[Section 3.6.3]{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} responds to these objections by contending that the inverse polynomial scaling allows their classes to capture algorithms like tomography and FPTASes.
However, if the goal is to build analogues to $\P$ and $\PSPACE$, the most fundamental and basic complexity classes, these choices are odd (for example, the knapsack problem is $\NP$-hard but also captured in $\uP$?), especially when they produce ill-behaved classes.
Though $\polylog(1/\eps)$ scaling is a strong guarantee, the most important unitary synthesis problems all meet it, including classical error reduction for decision problems, Hamiltonian simulation, and QSVT~\cite{gslw18}.

\paragraph{``quantum computer'':}

We model quantum algorithms as quantum circuits consisting of unitary gates.
In the case of $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$, this is necessary for the definition to make sense, because non-unitary channels do not maintain a meaningful notion of global phase.
For $\puP$, this is without loss of generality, because non-unitary gates can be replaced by unitary dilations at the cost of at most a polynomial increase in the number of qubits.
However, the situation for $\puPSPACE$ is less obvious, because purifying the computation would blow up the space complexity by an exponential.
As it turns out, there is a nontrivial method to purify a non-unitary implementation of a unitary transformation while maintaining polynomial space (see \Cref{rmk:pspace_purification} for details).
Thus it is without loss of generality to make all of the gates unitary, which we do for aesthetic simplicity.

We further assume the gates have explicitly-given entries with a \emph{fully polynomial time exponential approximation scheme} (FPTEAS), roughly meaning that they can be any numbers whose digits are computable in polynomial time.
Our choice borrows from Kuperberg~\cite{Kup15-jones}, who suggested the definition after observing that uncomputable gate entries can yield broken definitions for the class $\class{PostBQP}$.
In fact, $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$ suffer from the same issue: if we allow a gate such as
\[
    R = \begin{bmatrix}
        1 \\ & e^{\ii \pi \alpha}
    \end{bmatrix}
\]
for some $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ with uncomputable digits, then $R$ can of course be implemented under this gate set, but no implementation over effectively-specified gates can approximate it to every precision.
This presents a problem for Zhandry's definition~\cite{Zha25-unitary-oracles}, who allows for arbitrary universal gates.

The problem can be addressed by fixing some gate set with algebraic entries such as H, CNOT, T, or by requiring the uniformity machine to specify all of the gate entries to finite precision.
Our choice to allow \textit{any} FPTEAS is convenient because it allows us to abstract away the details of compilation into a fixed gate set, while still allowing access to gates with irrational algebraic entries such as the Hadamard gate.
For comparison, Zhandry's assumption of an arbitrary universal gate set leads to the annoyance of having to keep track of circuit compilation in every proof.
Under that definition, operations as simple as replacing a circuit by its complex conjugate require recompiling the entire circuit and accounting for the error incurred.

\paragraph{Oracles and reductions:}

Upon defining $\uP$ and $\uPSPACE$, the last step is to augment the classes to allow oracle access to a unitary language, in order to have a meaningful notion of composability.
A first try would be to simply allow circuits to apply elements $U$ of the language provided to it; this is how~\cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann} handle oracles.
However, this is a fairly weak type of access: many kinds of subroutines, including QSVT~\cite{gslw18}, amplitude amplification~\cite{BHMT02-amp}, and phase estimation~\cite{kitaev95}, also demand access to $U^\dagger$, $\controlled U$, or $\controlled U^\dagger$.
It is reasonable to grant these demands, as any circuit to instantiate the oracle also immediately provides circuits for these alternative oracles.

Zhandry~\cite{Zha25-unitary-oracles} goes even further, arguing that one should provide access to the more obscure $U^T$ and $U^*$, since the same logic goes for them, and they are, in a formal sense, the \textit{complete} list of oracles which need to be granted following this logic.
In our definitions, we follow Zhandry's generality, with the exception that for $\puP$ and $\puPSPACE$, we do not (and indeed, cannot) give access to the controlled unitaries, as this would lift an undistinguished global phase to a distinguishable relative phase.

Deciding which oracles to choose for the definition was another topic of contention among the authors.
Ultimately, we decided it was best to opt for the most permissive definition of oracles.
As a counterpoint, there are settings where the oracle is not instantiated by a circuit, but instead by nature, or another party keeping their circuit secret, or some other manner where one does not have access to all possible modified oracles.
However, like many contentions, this one is fairly inconsequential: our results hold regardless of what one takes oracle access to mean, with the exception that both $U$ and $U^\dagger$ seem to be required.

Our notion of oracle leads to one more issue which must be addressed: it might appear that $\puPSPACE$ is not self-low.
After all, if an oracle is called exponentially many times, and we instantiate the oracle with a circuit that leaves garbage after every call, then the garbage would appear to pile up and eventually exceed the polynomial space of a unitary circuit!
We avoid this issue by showing that given forward and inverse access to a dilation of an $n$-qubit unitary $U$, one can simulate arbitrarily many calls to $U$ while only holding at most $n$ qubits of garbage at any stage.

\section{Technical overview and further results}

Here we outline the progression of the paper in rough chronological order, making note of several other noteworthy results that we obtain along the way to our main theorems.

\subsection{Comparing unitary and projective unitary classes}

It might seem unsatisfactory or even elusive that we supply two sets of definitions rather than settling upon a single ``correct'' one.
While a valid concern, it turns out that the two notions of efficient unitary computation (with and without garbage) are more closely related than they might seem.
In fact, both definitions can be viewed as special cases of each other!
Concretely, we show:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:u_garbage_iff_u_udag_tidy}, informal]
    \label{thm:garbage_iff_informal}
    $\calU \in \puP$ if and only if $\calU \otimes \calU^\dagger \in \uP$.
\end{theorem}

And conversely:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:u_tidy_iff_cu_garbage}, informal]
    \label{thm:control_iff_informal}
    $\calU \in \uP$ if and only if $\controlled\calU \in \puP$.
\end{theorem}

Taken together, we see that one could use either $\uP$ or $\puP$ when proving some result, because any statement involving one class has an equivalent reformulation in terms of the other.
Thus, one should feel free to choose whichever definition is more convenient.
Typically, this will be $\uP$, because juggling garbage states is more cumbersome.

In the proof of \Cref{thm:garbage_iff_informal}, the more interesting direction is the forward one.
The basic idea is that if $C$ implements a dilation of $U$ with garbage state $\ket{g}$, then running $C$ \textit{backwards} with $\ket{g}$ as the ancilla both applies $U^\dagger$ and erases the garbage.
For \Cref{thm:control_iff_informal}, again the nontrivial direction is from $\puP$ to $\uP$.
Since $\controlled U$ always has the all-zeros state as an eigenstate, one can again run $C$ backwards on an all-zero input to erase the garbage.
Both theorems additionally hold with $\P$ replaced by $\PSPACE$, or relative to quantum oracles (or both); see \Cref{sec:garbage_tidy_relations} for details.

Interestingly, one can also show:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:u_garbage_iff_u_ustar_tidy}, informal]
    \label{thm:garbage_star_informal}
    $\calU \in \puP$ if and only if $\calU \otimes \calU^* \in \uP$.
\end{theorem}

So \Cref{thm:garbage_star_informal} looks the same as \Cref{thm:garbage_iff_informal}, but with the conjugate transpose replaced by just the complex conjugate!
In hindsight, this possibility should not surprise us, as both $U \otimes U^\dagger$ and $U \otimes U^*$ are examples of canonical unitary transformations that ``forget'' the global phase information in $U$.
(By contrast, note that $U \otimes U^\trans$ is \textit{not} phase-independent.)
The proof idea once again is to erase garbage using a known eigenstate.
Specifically, we use the fact that the maximally-entangled state $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x \in \{0,1\}^n} \ket{x}\ket{x}$ is a $1$-eigenstate of $U \otimes U^*$ for any $n$-qubit $U$.

\subsection{Characterizing space-bounded unitary computation}

For polynomial-\textit{space} computation, we establish an even tighter connection between the unitary and projective-unitary definitions.
In particular, we prove that one can generically erase garbage:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv}, informal]
    \label{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal}
    $\calU \in \puPSPACE$ if and only if there exists a $\calV \in \uPSPACE$ that equals $\calU$ up to global phase.
\end{theorem}

\Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal} is the strongest possible equivalence, because a unitary language $\calU \in \puPSPACE$ may encode uncomputable information in the phases, and therefore we cannot directly conclude $\calU \in \uPSPACE$.
Still, \Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal} is general enough to justify using only $\uPSPACE$ when proving statements about space-efficient unitary computation, as it says we can always assign \textit{some} global phase that makes the unitary computable cleanly.

Perhaps more useful than \Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal} itself is the proof by which we obtain it.
The key insight is that $\uPSPACE$ has an equivalent characterization in terms of the computability of its entries:

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization}, informal]
    \label{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal}
    $\calU \in \uPSPACE$ if and only if each entry of the $n$-qubit unitary in $\calU$ can be approximated to error $\eps$ in space $\poly(n, \log 1/\eps)$.
\end{theorem}

\Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal}
yields \Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal} by combining with the equivalence
\[
\calU \in \puPSPACE \iff \calU \otimes \calU^\dagger \in \uPSPACE, \qquad (\mathrm{\Cref{thm:garbage_iff_informal}})
\]
observing that we can use the entries of $\calU \otimes \calU^\dagger$ to compute the entries of $\calU$ up to a canonical global phase of our choice.

For the proof of \Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal}, the forward direction is essentially a consequence of the equivalence $\BQPSPACE = \PSPACE$~\cite{Wat99-space,Wat03-space,FR21-space}.
That is, for \textit{decision} problems, quantum and classical polynomial space are equivalent.
So, it suffices to find a polynomial-space quantum algorithm to estimate the entries of $\calU$, which amplitude estimation accomplishes~\cite{BHMT02-amp}.
For the reverse direction, we first use \textit{state synthesis}~\cite{GR02-state-prep,Aar16-barbados,INNRY22-qma-search} to show that we can space-efficiently prepare any column of $\calU$, given access to the entries.
Then, we appeal to a proof by Rosenthal~\cite{Ros21-unitary} that turns a $\calU$-column constructor into an implementation of $\calU$, with polynomial space overhead.

Of note, when working toward the proof of \Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal}, we find it helpful to work with certain unitary languages that encode real numbers in the entries.
In particular, we will frequently use the following definition of a \textit{phase encoding}:

\begin{definition}[Restatement of \Cref{def:fphase}]
    Let $f : \{0,1\}^* \to [-\pi/2, \pi/2]$.
    The \emph{phase encoding of $f$} is the unitary language $f\Phase = \{R_{f,n}\}_{n \in \N}$ defined by
    \[
    R_{f,n}\ket{x}
    =
    e^{i f(x)}\ket{x},
    \]
    for every $x \in \{0,1\}^n$.
\end{definition}

Phase estimation~\cite{kitaev95,NC10-book} almost immediately implies that the ability to implement $f\Phase$ is tightly connected to the approximability of $f$:

\begin{lemma}[\Cref{lem:rotation_to_fqpseas}, informal]
    $f\Phase \in \uPSPACE$ if and only if $f(x)$ can be approximated to error $\eps$ in space $\poly(|x|, \log 1/\eps)$.
\end{lemma}

When $f\Phase \in \uPSPACE$, it is particularly convenient to treat $f\Phase$ as an oracle within another $\uPSPACE$ algorithm, because we do not need to account for approximation errors when querying it; the self-lowness proof of $\uPSPACE$ handles this directly!
We defer to \Cref{sec:characterization} for the full details, but emphasize that phase encodings are an abstraction whose utility and convenience only became apparent to us in light of the composability of $\uPSPACE$.
See \Cref{lem:entry_to_column} for a particularly illustrative example of the elegant proofs that our definitions afford.

We conclude our discussion of $\uPSPACE$ by remarking that \Cref{thm:projunitarypspace_equiv_informal} also holds relative to classical oracles, but provably \textit{fails} relative to quantum oracles!

\begin{theorem}[\Cref{thm:no_global_phase}, informal]
    \label{thm:no_global_phase_informal}
    There is a unitary language $\calU$ such that for every unitary language $\calV$ that equals $\calU$ up to global phase, we have $\calV \not\in \uPSPACE^{\calU \otimes \calU^\dagger}$.
\end{theorem}

On the other hand, we clearly have $\calU \in \puP^{\calU \otimes \calU^\dagger}$, because the action of the $\calU^\dagger$ part of the oracle can be taken as the garbage state $\ket{g}$.
The proof of \Cref{thm:no_global_phase_informal} hinges on an observation made by Gavorov\'{a}, Seidel, and Touati~\cite{gst24} that there is no continuous map from the projective unitary group $PU(N)$ to the unitary group $U(N)$ that assigns a global phase to every projective unitary.
Moreover, \Cref{thm:no_global_phase_informal} relies on very little about $\uPSPACE$ other than the fact that it must approximately implement $\calV$ with a finite number of queries to $\calU \otimes \calU^\dagger$ (see \Cref{rmk:topology}).
Thus, \Cref{thm:no_global_phase_informal} shows that relative to unitary oracles, erasing garbage is generally impossible, and $\puP$ can be strictly more powerful than \textit{any} ``clean'' unitary class!

\subsection{Relation to unitary synthesis}

At last, we may return to the results described in \Cref{sec:this_work}.
Recall our key lemma:

\lemintrokey*

The entrywise characterization of $\uPSPACE$ (\Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal}) makes the proof of \Cref{lem:all-fnexp-informal} particularly simple.
Suppose that the first item fails, in which case there exists a classical language $L$ for which $\calU \in \uP^L$.
We construct an $\NEXP$ machine that expects a witness $w$ interpreted as an assignment to $L(x)$ on all strings $x$ of polynomial length.
Given $w$, the $\NEXP$ verifier simulates the $\uP^L$ algorithm in exponential time by brute-force matrix multiplication, replacing oracle queries according to $w$.
The verifier uses \Cref{thm:entrywise_characterization_informal} to compute $\calU$ entrywise and compares to the unitary implemented by the $\uP$ oracle machine, accepting if and only if they are sufficiently close.
Then, any witness $w$ that causes the $\NEXP$ machine to accept allows the $\uP$ machine to implement $\calU$, given oracle access to $w$.
This is to say that $\calU \in \uP^\FNEXP$, where $\FNEXP$ denotes $\NEXP$ witness search.

The remaining results about $\uPSPACE$ follow by combining \Cref{lem:all-fnexp-informal} with known facts from classical complexity theory.
For example, \Cref{cor:am_nexp_informal} follows immediately from the easy witness lemma of Impagliazzo, Kabanets, and Wigderson~\cite{IKW02-easy-witness}, which shows that if $\AM = \NEXP$, then bits of accepting $\NEXP$ witnesses can be computed in $\EXP = \PSPACE$.
\Cref{cor:nc_np_informal} follows from a similar statement that if $\NC = \NP$, then bits of accepting $\NEXP$ witnesses can be computed in $\EXP = \PSPACE$.
Indeed, this is because $\PSPACE$ and $\NEXP$ are essentially just ``exponentially scaled up'' versions of $\NC$ and $\NP$, respectively.
Though, what is noteworthy in \Cref{cor:nc_np_informal} is that the equivalence of $\NC$ and $\NP$ leads to a collapse of $\NEXP$ to $\PSPACE$ \textit{relative to any oracle}, as long as the $\NEXP$ queries are only on strings of polynomial length.
This is why \Cref{cor:am_nexp_informal} and \Cref{cor:nc_np_informal} relativize differently.

Finally, the connection to quantum commitments (\Cref{thm:main-informal}) results from proving that commitments cannot exist if $\uP = \uPSPACE$.
This was essentially established in \cite{BEMPQY26-uhlmann}, though we reprove it ourselves to ensure consistency with our definitions.
We use the fact that commitment schemes are equivalent to the existence of an \textit{EFI pair}: a pair of efficiently-generated density matrices $\rho_0$, $\rho_1$ that are far in trace distance, but computationally indistinguishable to polynomial-time quantum adversaries~\cite{BCQ23-efi,Yan22-commitments}.
Using the entrywise characterization of $\uPSPACE$, we show that $\uPSPACE$ can approximately implement the statistically optimal measurement to distinguish $\rho_0$ and $\rho_1$.
Consequently, $\uP = \uPSPACE$ would violate the security of the EFI pair against polynomial time adversaries.

\subsection{Discussion}

This work is heavy on conceptual contributions.
To name just a few, we show or argue that:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item Proving the existence of computationally-secure quantum cryptography is as hard as longstanding open problems in complexity theory.
    \item The unitary synthesis problem explicitly relates unitary complexity theory, classical complexity theory, and cryptography.
    \item Sensible definitions of unitary complexity classes require polylogarithmic error dependence.
    \item Unitary complexity theory does not have to be ugly; our definitions yield many elegant proofs.
    \item Notions of unitary implementation with and without garbage are each interesting and meaningfully related to one another.
    \item $\uPSPACE$ is a particularly robust class, having a simple entrywise characterization and generically allowing garbage erasure.
\end{enumerate}

In the era of AI-automated theory research, we believe these insights are comparatively valuable, as today's LLMs have superhuman capabilities in proving theorems but still struggle to extract big ideas or meaning.

The most concrete and natural problem left open by our work is whether polynomial-time unitary implementations can always erase garbage:

\begin{question}[Garbage erasure]
    \label{q}
    For every $\calU \in \puP$, is there a $\calV \in \uP$ that equals $\calU$ up to phase?
\end{question}

Versions of \Cref{q} have been raised before, implicitly by Aaronson~\cite[Question 3.3.2]{Aar16-barbados} and more explicitly by Rosenthal~\cite[Open Problem 1]{Ros23-thesis}, but to our knowledge there has been no meaningful progress toward answering \Cref{q}.
We showed a negative answer to \Cref{q} relative to a unitary oracle (\Cref{thm:no_global_phase_informal}), but we do not consider this particularly strong evidence in favor of a negative answer to the general question, because we are not even aware of a \textit{candidate} unitary language that separates the two classes in the unrelativized setting.

For a more open-ended direction, we consider it interesting to explore the other possible consequences of unitary synthesis for cryptography.
To give one example, we showed that a positive solution to unitary synthesis is sufficient for quantum cryptography to imply breakthrough classical lower bounds.
But could a \textit{negative} solution to unitary synthesis also cause quantum cryptography to yield classical circuit lower bounds?
In particular, suppose we had an EFI pair that were an ``explicit'' counterexample to the unitary synthesis conjecture, in the sense that any oracle-assisted quantum algorithm that breaks the cryptosystem must have superpolynomial complexity.
Would the existence of such an ``explicit'' hard EFI pair \textit{itself} have important classical consequences?

\section{Preliminaries}

\subsection{Quantum circuits}
We begin by defining a notion of approximation that will be used extensively in this work.
This definition borrows from Kuperberg~\cite{Kup15-jones}.

\begin{definition}[FPTEAS/FPSEAS]
    \label{def:fpteas}
    An encoding function $f: \{0,1\}^* \to \R$ has a \emph{fully polynomial time exponential approximation scheme}, or \textit{FPTEAS} for short, if there is a polynomial-time Turing machine $M$ whose output $\phi = M(x, \eps)$ satisfies $\abs{\phi - f(x)} \le \eps$, where $\phi$ and $\eps$ are encoded in fixed-point binary.\footnote{We will always assume $\eps = 2^{-\lambda}$ for some $\lambda \in \N$ without loss of generality, as for larger inputs one can run the algorithm with $\eps = 1$.}

    A \emph{fully polynomial space exponential approximation scheme} (\textit{FPSEAS}) is defined the same way, but where $M$ is a polynomial-\underline{space} Turing machine, and the output has polynomial length.
\end{definition}

Note that the time or space bound on $M$ is $\poly(|x|, \log 1/\eps)$.
Some examples of numbers that admit an FPTEAS encoding are all numbers that have a fixed-point binary representation (i.e., dyadic rationals) and all algebraic numbers.
If we are willing to modify the encoding slightly, it is also without loss of generality to take $M$ to be any universal Turing machine.

    

Also following Kuperberg~\cite{Kup15-jones}, we use FPTEAS encodings to specify gates in a quantum circuit.

\begin{definition}[Quantum circuit]
    \label{def:quantum_circuit}
    A \emph{quantum circuit} is a finite sequence of gates acting on qubits, in which each gate is specified by
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item the list of $k$ qubits it acts on, and
        \item a CPTP map on $2^k \times 2^k$ density matrices, described by an FPTEAS encoding $f$ of its matrix representation on the operator basis $\{\ketbra{i}{j}\}_{i, j \in [2^k]}$.
        That is, a channel $\Lambda$ is specified by the matrix $S$ with entries $S_{ij,k\ell} = \bra{i}\Lambda(\ketbra{k}{\ell})\ket{j}$, and each complex entry $a + bi$ of $S$ is described by a pair $x, y \in \{0,1\}^*$ for which $f(x) = a$ and $f(y) = b$.
    \end{enumerate}
\end{definition}

The description length of a circuit is the total length of the gate descriptions together with the qubit labels on which the gates act.
We treat each gate description as specifying an exact channel, even though its entries may only be accessed computationally through approximations.

Allowing entries with an FPTEAS means that we may exactly specify gates such as rotations by rational multiples of $2\pi$ and Fourier transforms.
Our definition abstracts away the details of compiling gates into a universal gate set and leaves it up to the algorithm to specify the precision of each gate, if applicable.

\begin{definition}[Unitary quantum circuit]
    \label{def:unitary_circuit}
    A quantum circuit is \textit{unitary} if each gate is a unitary superoperator $\rho \to U\rho U^\dagger$ specified by the $2^k \times 2^k$ unitary matrix $U$ (with explicit global phase).
\end{definition}

Every $n$-qubit unitary circuit defines a unitary matrix in $\C^{2^n \times 2^n}$ (with explicit global phase) obtained by taking the product of the unitaries.

We also define classical oracle-augmented quantum circuits in the standard way:

\begin{definition}[Oracle quantum circuit]
    For a language $L$, an \emph{$L$-oracle quantum circuit} is a sequence that may contain both explicitly specified $k$-qubit gates (as above) and $n$-qubit oracle gates $U_n$ for the language $L$, which act unitarily as
    \[
    U_n\ket{x, b} = \ket{x, b \oplus L(x)}
    \]
    for every $x \in \{0,1\}^{n-1}$ and $b \in \{0,1\}$.
    These oracle gates are specified only by the qubits acted upon.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Uniform circuit family]
    A family $\{C_x\}_{x \in \{0,1\}^*}$ of quantum circuits is \textit{time-uniform} if there exists a polynomial-time Turing machine $M$ with a write-only output tape such that $M(x)$ outputs a description of $C_x$.

    A \textit{space-uniform} family is defined the same way, but with a polynomial-\underline{space} machine $M$, and with the restriction that each gate has a polynomial-length description.\footnote{For example, we do not want to allow the space-uniform machine to output a gate whose FPTEAS encoding is exponentially long.
    We want each gate in the circuit to be storable in polynomial memory.}

When a circuit family is indexed by several parameters, such as $\{C_{n, \eps}\}_{n \in \N, \eps > 0}$, we regard it as a family indexed by a single binary string encoding those parameters.

title: Hamiltonian locality testing and certification do not achieve the Heisenberg limit
abstract: We establish lower bounds for Hamiltonian property testing with access to the time-evolution operator but not its inverse. Each experiment may query the time-evolution operator multiple times, and distances between Hamiltonians are measured in the normalized Frobenius norm. In this model, we show that testing whether a Hamiltonian is $k$-local or $\varepsilon$-far from every $k$-local Hamiltonian requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Kallaugher and Liang (TQC'25). We also prove that testing whether an unknown Hamiltonian equals a target Hamiltonian or is $\varepsilon$-far from it requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, matching the upper bound of Sinha and Tong (2025). These are the first lower bounds for natural problems in Hamiltonian learning and testing that rule out Heisenberg-limited scaling of $1/\varepsilon$. As a third result, we show that amplitude estimation to precision $\varepsilon$ requires $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total time evolution, recovering the result of Tang and Wright (QIP'26) in the continuous-time query model. All three results follow from the hardness of distinguishing the zero Hamiltonian from a suitably chosen ensemble of random Hamiltonians. We establish this hardness by adapting the continuous-time adversary method to forward Hamiltonian evolution.
summary:
**TL;DR** This paper proves the first Ω(1/ε²) total-evolution-time lower bounds for natural Hamiltonian testing problems in the forward-only (no inverse, no controlled access) time-evolution access model, showing that Hamiltonian locality testing and Hamiltonian certification in normalized Frobenius distance *cannot* reach the Heisenberg 1/ε scaling. The same technique reproves the Ω(1/ε²) lower bound for amplitude estimation with forward-only queries, now in the stronger continuous-time (fractional-query) model. All three follow from one technical result: there is an ensemble of random diagonal Hamiltonians with mean-zero, variance-ε² entries that needs Ω(1/ε²) evolution time to distinguish from the zero Hamiltonian.

**The big picture** A central goal in characterizing quantum hardware is to learn or verify the interactions governing a device by letting it evolve and measuring the outcome, and a large literature has shown that clever protocols can reach the optimal precision-versus-time tradeoff dictated by quantum metrology. This work shows that limit is not universal: for two natural verification tasks — checking whether an unknown interaction only couples few particles at a time, and checking whether it matches a known target — the metrological speedup is provably unavailable when you can only run time forward. The proof imports the adversary method from quantum query complexity into the continuous-time Hamiltonian setting, giving the field a new lower-bound tool where previously essentially none existed beyond the metrological bound.

**Key contributions**
- Matching Ω(1/ε²) lower bound for k-local testing (for k ≤ n/8, ε² ≥ 24·2⁻ⁿ), matching Kallaugher–Liang's upper bound.
- Matching Ω(1/ε²) for certification against a known target (ε² ≥ 3·2⁻ⁿ⁻¹), answering negatively Bluhm et al.'s question of whether locality assumptions were an artifact.
- Ω(1/ε²) for amplitude estimation in the continuous-time forward-query model, strengthening Tang–Wright.
- Adaptation of the continuous-time adversary method to forward-only Hamiltonian evolution, with an explicitly constructed progress function rather than an invocation of a general theorem.

**How it works** Diagonal Hamiltonians with Boolean entries correspond exactly to fractional phase queries, motivating query-complexity machinery. The hard ensemble has iid entries drawn from the spectral measure ν_ε of a block operator J_ε = [[0, ε⟨b|],[ε|b⟩, M]] acting on C⊕L²([−½,½]), where M is multiplication by ω and b a smooth normalized bump. This gives E[h]=0, E[h²]=ε², |h|≤1, so the ensemble is ε-far with constant probability. Crucially, the spread-out spectrum kills the easy attack: the ±ε ensemble satisfies U_H(π/ε)=−I and is distinguishable in O(1/ε) time by a Hadamard test (controlization is free). The adversary argument purifies the randomness into registers, and uses the two decay estimates ∫₀^∞|⟨b|e^{−iMτ}|b⟩|dτ ≤ C and ∫₀^∞|⟨b|e^{−iMτ}|r⟩|²dτ ≤ C_obs‖r‖² (from integration by parts and Plancherel) to build a correction operator G from convolution operators O, R, D. The progress function P(t)=1−Re⟨Ψ_Z|Ψ_F⟩+¼⟨Ψ_F|I⊗G|Ψ_F⟩ starts at 0, must reach Ω(1), and has derivative O(ε²λ(t)).

**Why it matters** Settles the complexity of Hamiltonian locality testing after several rounds of upper bounds, and delineates where Heisenberg scaling genuinely lives: structure (locality/sparsity) in *both* the target and the unknown, not just forward access, is what buys 1/ε.

**Caveats** Bounds require ε not exponentially small (1/ε = 2^{O(n)}); the exact constant c such that ε = 2^{−cn} still works is open, and the concurrent Fourier-analytic work of Allen et al. obtains Ω(√d/ε) in the high-precision regime, which the authors say their method can also recover. Hard instances are diagonal, so the bounds say nothing about restricted (e.g. geometrically local) Hamiltonian classes; sparsity testing remains open.

title: On The Complexity of Redundancy-Free Quantum Hamiltonians
abstract: We consider a class of redudancy-free Hamiltonians, which are those where the trace vanishes for any product of Hamiltonian terms in which at least one term appears an odd number of times. This includes Hamiltonians which are sums of products of Paulis with no relations between them. These Hamiltonians arise naturally in Hamiltonian Decoded Quantum Interferometry, which separates the hardness of preparing quantum states into two steps: a classical decoding step, and a step preparing the thermofield double state of such a redundancy-free Hamiltonian. We focus on the hardness of these Hamiltonians, both for intrinsic interest and to understand the complexity of the state preparation step in Hamiltonian DQI. We present several results showing that the problem becomes easy at quadratically lower temperature than for a general Hamiltonian, with the complexity at given inverse temperature $β$ depending on $β^2 d$, where $d$ is the degree of the anticommutation graph. We give an efficient classical algorithm for small $β^2 d$ to approximate the partition function, while for large $β^2 d$ we show that approximating the partition function is NP-hard. To this end, we introduce what we call an anticommutation glass, where frustration arises purely from anticommutation relations. We give a subexponential time quantum algorithm to prepare the thermofield state for small $β^2 d$, and present some results toward a polynomial time algorithm based on the Feiguin-Klich Hamiltonian. As a result of possible independent interest, we show that this Hamiltonian leads to a polynomial time algorithm for preparing thermofield double states of general Hamiltonians on an interaction graph of degree $d$ for $β\lesssim 1/d$. Finally, we show that estimating the ground state energy of redundancy-free Hamiltonians is QMA-complete.
summary:
**TL;DR** This paper maps the complexity landscape of "redundancy-free" Hamiltonians — sums of terms where any product containing a term an odd number of times is traceless (e.g. independent Pauli products) — and shows the controlling parameter is $\kappa=\beta^2 d$ ($d$ = degree of the anticommutation graph), not $\beta d$ as for generic Hamiltonians. A convergent polymer expansion gives a classical algorithm for the partition function at small $\kappa$, while at large $\kappa$ approximating the partition function is NP-hard (and ground-state energy estimation is QMA-complete), via a new "anticommutation glass" in which frustration comes purely from anticommutation.

**The big picture** A recent quantum algorithm splits the hard problem of preparing thermal states of quantum systems into a classical decoding step and the preparation of a special purified thermal state whose only structure is which terms commute or anticommute. How hard that second step is was the main open question. This work shows that stripping away all algebraic redundancy among the terms genuinely buys you something: the easy regime extends to temperatures quadratically lower than for generic systems, but not further — beyond that threshold, anticommutation alone is enough to manufacture glassy frustration and worst-case hardness.

**Key contributions**
- Polymer (cluster) expansion whose convergence hinges on every term appearing an even number of times, yielding convergence at $\beta\sim 1/\sqrt{d}$ rather than $1/d$; truncation at total support $W_{\rm tot}\sim\log(n/\epsilon)/\log(1/\kappa)$ gives runtime $O(n(n/\epsilon)^{O(\log d/\log \kappa^{-1})})$.
- The *anticommutation glass*: two commuting families ($X_i$ and $D_i=\prod_j Z_j^{A_{ij}}$, $A$ invertible over $\mathbb F_2$) with two competing "basins", supported by series expansion, path-integral QMC (with a non-local move flipping a single $Z$-type operator; hysteresis observed at $n=200$), and a toy two-level model where collective hopping/diagonal splitting $\sim\kappa^{-1/2}$.
- Formal NP-hardness: glasses on cubic graph vertices, ancilla-dressed couplings encoding MAXCUT; explicit matrices $A_v(x,y)=\delta_{xy}+\mathrm{tr}_{\mathbb F}(\alpha_v xy)$ over $\mathbb F_{4^s}$ with a 4-coloring; $n/2-1\le d\le 7n$, $\beta=\Theta(d^{-1/2})$, factor-2 approximation of the normalized $\mathcal Z$ is NP-hard.
- QMA-completeness of ground-state energy for redundancy-free Hamiltonians.
- Subexponential quantum TFD preparation at small $\kappa$; plus, of independent interest, a Feiguin–Klich-based polynomial-time TFD preparation for *general* degree-$d$ Hamiltonians at $\beta\lesssim 1/d$ with no lattice-dimension dependence (unlike prior work).
- HDQI robustness: pilot-state infidelity and decoder failure add ($D_{\rm tr}\le\sqrt{\varepsilon_p}+\sqrt{2r/\delta}$ for random signs), and $\mu_\beta$ is local-stochastic with rates $(\beta J_i/2)^2$ — quadratically better in $\beta$ than the generic polynomial-filter scheme.

**Why it matters** It identifies the precise temperature threshold at which HDQI's quantum step stops being easy, delimiting where the algorithm can plausibly give advantage, and introduces a clean model of purely anticommutation-induced glassiness.

**Caveats** The lower-bound construction needs degree growing with block size, so hardness is at $\beta=\Theta(d^{-1/2})$ with block $n$ fixed independent of graph size; the small-$\kappa$ classical algorithm is polynomial only for fixed $d,\kappa$. The glass's two-basin physics rests partly on numerics that visibly fail to equilibrate, and no polynomial-time quantum TFD algorithm is obtained at $\beta\lesssim 1/\sqrt d$ — a gap left open, along with whether effective *quantum* Ising models can be encoded.
